speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: I must remind hon. members that the House is not in committee, and that therefore the questions which are now being asked of the hon. minister are not strictly relevant to the discussion before the House. We are discussing the powers to be given to a committee; we are certainly not discussing the administration of the Canadian National railways.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I say on that point of order, Mr. Speaker, that the minister affirmed that no information was refused to the House? In that respect he was subject to correction.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
If I made any statements that the hon. member thinks are not correct, of course he can make any reply he wishes. But the statements that I am making now are absolutely correct. Now, another impression that I would get from the speech of the hon. leader of the Opposition is that he would like it to go out to the public that the loss of $49,000,000 last year was, through interference by the Government increased this year to $70,000,000. If the hon. gentleman wishes to do justice to the operation of the Canadian National railways, in the public interest he should have also stated what he knows
himself, for he has had it told him in this House and in the press, that some of the causes for this great increase in the deficit were: First, the McAdoo award, which compelled the railways of Canada to further increase the wages of their employees, and that increase being retroactive, the Canadian Government railways, if my memory serves me right, had to pay about $20,000,000 to its employees for the period between the first of May and the first of September,-a period during which there was no possible chance of getting any increased return from traffic, because the increased freight rates took effect only on September 1. Second, there is a very heavy increase in operating costs on account of the greatly enhanced price of fuel; the hon. leader of the Opposition knew this also. Third, during last year the Canadian National railways had to do exactly what the Canadian Pacific railway bad to do, that is, increase the expenditure on maintenance, in other words, attend to what is called deferred maintenance; this also the leader of the Opposition knew. We had to expend a very large amount on that account, which, of course, is charged to operation. When those several amounts are taken into account, the reason for the greater deficit is obvious, and but for these additional expenditures the loss in operation would not have been as much this year as for the previous year's operation.
Another impression needs to be corrected. One would think that the taking over of the operation of the Canadian Northern railway means that that railway is losing $70,000,000. But the leader of the Opposition knows that $20,000,000 of that loss is caused by the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that $7,000,000, for the reason I have given here, is caused by the operation of the Transcontinental; or a total of $27,000,000 of that loss is due to the policy of the leader of the Opposition and his party when they were in power.

Mr. Speaker, may I rise to a point of order in view of the ruling which was given at the beginning of this discussion? I have no objection at all to the minister continuing along that line, but it must be understood that we will be at liberty to follow him. At the very opening of the debate the Speaker ruled that the question of the policy and the history of the national railways, and particularly the question of responsibility for the present conditions, were not to be discussed. The minister is now discussing them. If he

i	.
desires to do that, well and good, but I think it should be clearly understood that we are to be allowed to follow him along that line.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am extremely anxious to have this committee appointed and, if it is necessary, to bring before it every member of the management who understands the railway situation, in the hope that we may find out from them if it is possible to operate our railways in any better way. I am anxious to let this House know, by the management explaining to the committee, why it is not in the interests of our national railway system, and, therefore, of the public, that some of the information-and it is only of very limited amount-should be given. I think that the statements about information not being furnished are hardly fair to the management or in the interests of the operation of this system. In every case I have endeavoured to give all the information that any hon. member has requested, unless the management honestly felt that it would not be in the public interest to give it. When we have this committee functioning, I am sure hon. members who are now criticising the management, as well as the Government, for not giving certain information will change their minds, and, instead of creating an impression throughout the country that the operation of the road is not being carried on in the public interest, they will join with us in trying to make it a success. With that co-operation, I am satisfied, the Canadian Northern Railway system, with all its subsidiary companies, will in a few years prove one of the greatest assets we have not only in the development of this country but in bringing down freight rates to the lowest possible point.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay this discussion. I am in favour of the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I do not understand all this wrangle about the motion in itself and the amendment which has been offered. But it is easy to understand why, under such circumstances, the parliamentary institutions of Canada are falling into disrepute. Facing as we do a problem of such appalling magnitude, it

seems to me, Sir, that all parties should unite with a view to seeing that light is freely given to the taxpayers of Canada on this vexed question.
I repeat that I do not understand this wrangle. Here is a motion moved by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), a motion granting a committee. It is rather involved and restricted in its terms. I hear the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) say: I am quite ready to accept the motion, provided the suggestion of the hon. leader of the Opposition is also accepted. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the two motions which are before you are complete in themselves, so to speak. The Prime Minister grants a special committee to investigate railway matters but restricts its powers, and the leader of the Opposition, by his motion, offers to widen the scope of the inquiry. I object to the action of Parliament being restricted in any way in connection with this proposed investigation. No one, so far has averred that there is anything sinister behind it. For my part, I know the general manager and president of the Canadian National Railways, and speaking with a sense of at least some responsibility I have nothing to reproach Mr. Hanna. I will go further and say that under the circumstances under which he was handed the management of our railway system, he was perhaps the only man available. I do not see, therefore, what there is to fear from the investigation. I do not like the style adopted by the right hon. Prime Minister in his motion. It is much too involved; and the scope of the investigation too much restricted. Why all this mystery, Mr. Speaker? What the people expect is a full investigation in order that we may know how we can get out of the terrible muddle in which we find ourselves. I agree, therefore, with the attitude taken this afternoon by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's; I support the principle of the motion of the Prime Minister, but the powers of the committee are not wide enough, and I accept the principle involved in the amendment, that of affording to Parliament all facilities necessary to a full inquiry.
Mr. Speaker, the House must face the issue squarely. The time has gone by when parties could play politics with such a grave situation; for my part, I do not intend to do so. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) had to confess the other day that he was face to face with a deficit of $70,000,000 in respect of the government-owned railways,

and one of the best informed heads of his department came out in the press next day stating that the real deficit is $138,000,000. This is a serious gap, and how can we know who speaks the truth in the matter and who does not? We have, as I said the other day, become so accustomed to dealing in millions and even billions during recent years that we have lost all sense of proportion. But the people are beginning to feel the pinch, and they are clamouring for a halt in that carnival of expenditure. It is useless for any hon. member on either side to re-open old sores. It is of no avail to use the old argument: You are another. Having sat in the House for twenty-five years, I am, with others, partly responsible for the situation in which the country finds itself to-day as regards the railway question, and I do not wish to shirk my responsibility. If I have erred, Mr. Speaker, I wish to improve matters. But in order to improve matters, we must find a solution- How shall we solve the problem if not by the experience and the wisdom of those experts who will be heard before the committee? But let us vest in that committee the necessary authority to examine thoroughly the books, the correspondence, the orders and the management generally of the whole system. Is that a fair attitude to take? I think it is.
I say further that Parliament must not only save the railway system of Canada; it must above all save the credit of the nation-for the national credit is involved in the solution of this problem. Why should not the Prime Minister, with all his ability and his undoubted courage-why should he not, as they say in England, "take the bull by the horns" and give this committee the fullest powers? What can we learn with such restricted powers as are outlined in this motion? If he maintains the attitude which he has taken, what will be the result of the investigation? A committee will be appointed composed of members from both sides of the House, and with the restriction of the scope of the inquiry there will be a lack of unanimity. The committee will submit a minority as well as a majority report. This will not be because either side refuse to shed light upon the subject, but because they will be prevented by the very wording of the motion itself from inquiring fully into the administration of the railway system. Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that we should secure a unanimous report from that committee. It should be composed of the best men on both sides of the House. I exclude myself at once; I have
but limited knowledge on railway matters. But the committee should be selected from the most experienced men in the ranks of the three parties, men who know and who can speak with authority. I am not afraid to trust hon. members on both sides if you give them the necessary power to probe this whole situation.
Just now, the situation is very much embroiled. You do not meet two men on the street, but they will at once ask you: "What are you going to do with the railway problem and where is Canada drifting?" You have only to throw up your hands, to shrug your shoulders; you do not know what will be or what can be done. My right hon. friend has accepted the idea propounded in this House by the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and he has granted at last a committee with a view to disentangle the problem.	Why not do
at once the right	thing? Why
not give that committee all the powers which Parliament ' has undoubtedly the right to grant? Parliament, we all know, is defined by the authorities as being the great inquest of the nation. I trust the wisdom, the patriotism of members on both sides of the House; I trust their good judgment, their loyalty to Canada, and I say that to give that committee the widest powers would not imperil the railway situation, as my right hon. friend seems to fear it would.
As I read to-day press reports from the other side, I hang my head in shame. When I see the bondholders of the Grand Trunk congregating at the various banking institutions in London, clamouring for their dividends and the rumour being spread throughtout Great Britain that Canada will not pay, I say that I hang my head in shame. This is the first time in the history of Canada that it is said, with some semblance of authority, that Canada does not meet her obligations. Do you not believe, Sir, that if the amendment of the leader of the Opposition is voted down if that committee is not given the widest powers, people in England, and in the United States will say: "Canada by its Government wishes to dodge the issue; does not face it squarely; there is something so rotten that the public must not know the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth." I say again: Give the widest powers to that committee.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that there is no sentiment in business, and that capital is easily frightened. Remember that if in 1849, the captains of industry in Canada

were shaken in their faith in their country, it was because'they realized that there was no sentiment in business. Let not the faith of the Canadian people be shaken in their institutions, if you wish to maintain this country as it has been maintained in the past. Sir, I am reminded, whilst we are witnessing in this chamber, the wrangle about the scope of the inquiry on the most momentous issue that has ever confronted the Canadian people, of the words of that great French orator at the time of the revolution, when to avoid a financial collapse, the states general were deliberating the urgency of levying a quarter of the national wealth of France: " Bankruptcy is at your door, and you are still deliberating." Far be it from me the thought that bankruptcy is at the door, but we are in a very serious crisis. We are facing the most complex situation that has ever confronted Canada, and when we are asking ' that the whole matter be probed to the bottom and a way found out of this trouble honourably for the credit of the country and to alleviate the burden of the tax payers we are stopped by a motion, involved, restricted in its terms. This is not the proper way to settle this difficulty. Again, I appeal to my right hon. friend to amend his motion, have it adopted unanimously by the House of Commons, then strike the strongest committee possible, go to work and thus relieve public anxiety.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) and the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) have, at any rate, this much in common, that they both propose reference to a committee, of matters relating to our Canadian National Railways and our Canadian Government Merchant Marine. In the discussion that took place in this House a few days ago upon a motion moved by the leader of the Opposition, I took the ground that the floor of Parliament was not the place to receive answers to questions relating to every detail of the administation of our national railways or merchant marine, nor was it the place in which to move for Orders for Returns in regard to any particular phase of the business or administration of those enterprises. At that time, I took the position that, in my judgment, the whole matter should be referred to a committee with power to make to this Parliament such recommendations as it saw fit. The reasons for that position to some degree at any

rate, I think I made clear at that time. If we are to have brought down in this House returns that will taring up discussions, going into every aspect of detail of the administration of those great enterprises to which this country is committed, I can see no possibility of securing efficient or successful management, for this reason, if for no other, that no self-respecting man, who has the capacity properly and adequately to manage those enterprises, will sit down under the cross-fire of debate in this House where, for political reasons, in the expectation possibly of political gain by either side of this House, his administration may be challenged, may be criticized, and he has not the power, nor the opportunity to make explanation or defence. No self-respecting management will submit to that, and consequently, the first essential, if we are to secure the efficiency in management which those enterprises require, is that we free the management from that possibility. But when I took that position, I took also the position that the matter should be referred to a committee and the opportunity given for full inquiry.
If I may refer again to what I was saying a moment ago, discussion of these details across the floor of this House will lead in itself to no useful purpose, nor give any effective aid to the solution of this question. Take the Canadian Pacific Railway, the best managed road for its size in the world, at the present time,-I think that claim can be made without fear of successful contradiction. But if you place the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the position that every detail of its business, every contract entered into, every purchase made, every station-house built, and the case of every man dismissed on the system, can be reviewed in Parliament, the efficiency that now exists in that corporation would not last for twenty-four hours. The railway would go down. Consequently, we must clear ourselves from this disability in the consideration of this great question. Now at the time I took the position I did, on the occasion of the resolution introduced by the leader of the Opposition, my hon. friend asked me a very definite question. He said:
Mr. Mackenzie King-: The hon. gentleman has intimated to the House that he is favourable to the resolution standing in the name of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) which is that these matters might be referred to a select committee. Is it my hon. friend's understanding in that connection that such a committee shall have the right to ask any ques-

tions with respect to these railways that may he thought in the public interest and have it answered?
Mr. Crerar: If I am in order in answering the question, Mr. Speaker, I would say that I certainly think so.
Having taken that position, I find myself now faced with the question of deciding between the motion moved by the leader of the Government, and the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition. The motion moved by the leader of the Government undoubtedly restricts the inquiry in some degree. I think that is clear. The difference between the motion and the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition lies in this, that the amendment of the leader of the Opposition embraces a wider scope of inquiry than the reference in the motion moved by the leader of the Government. Now, it does seem to me that when this matter is referred to the committee, it would be wise to give the committe power to inquire into any phase or aspect of the business that in its judgment may be deemed advisable, and I understand that this is the purpose of the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Believing that, I shall support the amendment. In all the discussions we have had on the railways in this House, we have had as yet very little in the nature of constructive suggestions as to how we shall overcome the difficulties that face us in reference to this business of railways and shipping. My hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) who spoke the other evening, did in my opinion offer a few constructive suggestions. I would like to see this committee when it gets to work, consider this question solely from the point of view of the national interest. Let us, if we can, drop all partisan spirit in connection with this matter. The criticism I have to offer, if I may offer it here now to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, is this, that while he has criticised a great deal so far, he has offered no constructive suggestions as to how this serious problem can be solved. If I may take the liberty of saying so, my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition runs some danger of leaving the impression on the country that he is more concerned with making political capital out of this problem than he is with finding a solution for it. I do hope, Sir, that when the committee come to consider this matter, they will approach it free from any spirit of that kind.
There are a great many matters that have to be settled in connection with the national railways. I shall not at this moment, because I do not think I should be strictly in Order to do so, attempt to discuss them, but when I face this fact, that last year our national railways lost $49,000,000, that this year the taxpayers of Canada are called upon to put up $70,000,000 to make good the fixed charges and operating deficit on the national roads, when I contemplate, as was indeed mentioned in this House the other evening that the loss for the coming year may be even greater, I am impressed with the gravity of the situation. To my mind the solution of this railway problem constitutes one of the greatest problems that this country has been called upon to solve in the last fifty years, and it cannot be solved unless it is approached by all with the single-minded purpose of finding the best solution of it. It must be approached as a business proposition. We are called upon to pay in Federal taxes in this country $582,000,000, for that is the amount the Government have placed in the Estimates now before Parliament, and there are still the Supplementary Estimates to be brought down; I venture to say that if the total burden of taxation on the Canadian people could be estimated-I have made no close estimate of it, because I have not had the facilities for doing so-I think it would be found that for federal, provincial, municipal, and school purposes the Canadian people are to-day paying little less than $1,000,000,000 a year. On top of that, we have annually to send out of this country from $225,000,000 to $250,000,000' for interest on investments in Canada from abroad. Whe,n we take all these facts into consideration, we cannot escape the gravity of the situation. I do hope that the members who compose this committee, when they get to work, will sit down with the single-minded purpose of finding the best possible solution for this question. And if they do, they can find it. There is no question so difficult that it cannot be solved, but this question can only be solved if we approach it with the high purpose and in the spirit which I am convinced the Canadian people are demanding of this Parliament to-day.
Right hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (King's, N.S.) : Mr. Speaker, I regard this motion which has been proposed by the Prime Minister as a very important one, but not altogether for the reasons which have been advanced by some hon. members who have addressed the House. There has

been from time to time, especially during the present session, the question raised as to the amount and character of information with respect to the operation and management of the Canadian National system of railways that ought to be afforded to the House of Commons in the public interest. I think every hon. gentleman who has addressed the House has realized that this is a question of very considerable concern not only to this Parliament but to the people of this country. The hon. member (Mr. Crerar) who has just addressed the House spoke in that sense the other day, and again this afternoon. I entirely agreed with the view which he expressed on both occasions, that if you are to drag the details of management of this system of railways into the discussions of this Parliament in every conceivable way, or even into the discussions of a committee of this House appointed for this purpose, you would not only place the operation of the system under a very grave handicap, but also find it exceedingly difficult to obtain a man with the requisite ability at the head of the management.
The next thing I have to say as to the position taken by my hon. friend the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) is this: He apparently is of the opinion that you ought to be able to do immediately in committee what, according to his own judgment, it would not be proper to do in the House of Commons. But I should like to remind him that if you once make these matters the property of a committee of this House you make them at once the property of the House itself, and every question which in his judgment ought not to be raised in this House would naturally come before the House, for the reason that it would have been raised and investigated by the committee. Therefore, I am disposed to think, with all respect, that the position which he took the other day in the House was the correct one, although not altogether consistent with the position he has taken to-day.
I regard this committee as of the highest possible importance. It is in the first place to define a principle which will be for the guidance not only of this Parliament but perhaps of other parliaments in the years to come. It is to define a principle according to which the Government of the day will be relieved from the invidious position of saying that this information may be accorded because it is in the public interest but that some other information shall not be accorded because it is not in that interimSir Robert Borden.]
est. I am sure my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) made it clear, both the other day and to-day, that he does not regard it as right or proper that the Government of this country should be the sole judge in that respect; and I certainly understood, when this motion was proposed the other day, and further, when it was moved this afternoon, that the purpose of the committee was not in the first place to make an investigation, but was, first of all, to define a principle, and thereafter the committee would proceed to make its investigation according to the principle so stated and fixed. It seems to me that the public interest would be perfectly and absolutely guarded if that were carried out, and it can certainly be carried out under the resolution as proposed by the right hon. the Prime Minister. But for the moment I am at a loss to see how it could be carried out if the House were to adopt the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). That amendment is based upon a principle, stated very frankly by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), that every item and every detail with regard to the operation of the Canadian National system of railways shall be brought up, and if necessary taken up in the House.

speechtext:
I suppose it is hardly worth while to confer upon a committee a power which it is not intended that that committee shall exercise. If we are to give power to the committee, our action to that end is surely in vain if the committee is not to exercise that power. It is intended that the committee shall exercise the power given it, and, moreover, it would be its duty so to do. I therefore venture to think that the proposal presented to the House by the Prime Minister is along right and sane lines, namely, to confer upon the committee, in the first instance, the

power and duty to establish a principle as to the information which may properly be brought down in the public interest, and then, having dealt with that question, to come to the House if need be for such further powers as will ensure that principle being carried into effect. So far as I am concerned, I propose to support the resolution which has been moved by the Prime Minister and to vote against the amendment proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, for the reason that the investigation ought not to precede the definition of the extent to which the committee shall go, but that the definition should first be made and then the investigation proceeded with along the line so fixed.
I should like to add one word further. There are many aspersions cast in these days upon the principle of national ownership, and very many gloomy forebodings as to what the future of the Canadian National system of railways will be. The efficient management of the Canadian National Railways will be a test of Canadian democracy, and I have a very confident hope that the spirit and intent of the Canadian democracy will make that management efficient. At the present time it is beyond question that we have a greater railway mileage in this country than our population can very well sustain. We embarked upon a project of three transcontinental railways with a small population-I think the United States had a population of forty millions before they embarked on the project of a second transcontinental line. We have not too great mileage for our area, although it is out of proportion to our population. But is there any hon. gentleman in this House, who has given attentive consideration to the question and who will not reach the conclusion that when our population doubles, when we have eighteen millions of people instead of nine millions, the Canadian National system of railways, if operated intelligently and efficiently, and free from partisan interference in the meantime, will be a great national asset in the years to come? I have no more doubt about that than I have of my own existence, and I hope-in this I echo the words of my hon. friend the member for Marquette-that both sides of the House, all parties in the House, will join in a sincere and earnest effort to give to that great system of railways the efficient, honest and unbiased administration that will make it a national asset of enormous value in the years to come.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when introducing his statement on the financial condition of our railways for the operating year ending 1920 the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) invited suggestions and co-operation from both sides of the House as to the best methods of extricating the system from the difficulties into which it had become involved. But in order to come to his assistance and to render him the help of which he stands so much in need, we require the information which we have sought to obtain by the many questions we have placed on the Order Paper. To some of these questions answers have been forthcoming, but as to the balance we have been refused any information. We have also made other attempts to obtain particulars. A resolution was introduced by the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the effect that documents and letters should be produced and witnesses summoned to inform the House in relation to our national railways. Later on the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) introduced a resolution to appoint a committee with full powers to summon witnesses and collect all necessary data. The Government prevailed on the hon. member to withdraw his motion and promised themselves to introduce a resolution for the creation of such a committee as that suggested by him. But, Sir, the resolution which is now the subject matter of this discussion will not fulfil the purpose that the hon. gentleman had in view. Far from giving to the House the required information, this resolution is one of those numerous side-tracking devices of the hon. Minister of Railways to dodge the issue and prevent the information sought from being laid before the House.
We have been accused this afternoon of introducing party politics into this matter. I think, Sir, that no accusation was less deserved by the Opposition. I do not believe there is a single hon. member, and surely not one on this side of the House, who is not desirous of treating this matter on broad national lines with a view to finding the best methods of getting the country out of this serious difficulty. I do not believe there, is a single member on this side of the House who is not sincerely anxious to help the Government, and who would not be glad to-day to be able to congratulate

the hon. minister on a profitable operation of the road during the past year. But the financial report presented by him is appalling. It shows that we are face to face with a deficit of at least $70,000,000. without taking into account $75,000,00 of bonds issued for the renewal of the rolling stock; and if we are to accept the statements of some of the employees the deficit is really $120,000,000 or $130,000,000. To any lover of his country this distressing situation immediately removes the question from the sphere of party politics. It can be treated only in the light of our national interests. And notwithstanding the taunts that the Opposition has been playing a party game on this great question, I am going to deal with it purely and simply in the light of our national interests.
To my mind, Sir, the crux of the whole question is not whether we shall derive any political gain by discussing it, but whether we can ascertain the best methods of helping the Government to get out of the difficulties in which they have become involved. To help the Government what must we have? We must have full information; the House must be put in possession of all the facts. How can we judge the question otherwise? We sit to-day as a tribunal. We are the representatives of the electors of this country, who are the shareholders of our national railways, and the Minister , of Railways, representing in this House the management of the system, has laid before us a financial statement which discloses a tremendous deficit.
Comparisons are made between the national railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. My hon. friends opposite say that they will not give us any fuller details than the Canadian Pacific Railway management would be willing to give to their shareholders. Sir, the position of the directorate of a company which comes before its shareholders with such a statement as that presented by the Minister of Railways is quite different from that of the directorate of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has presented to its shareholders a financial statement showing a substantial surplus on the year's operations, the result of sound and progressive management. Were the minister in a position to lay before us a financial statement similar to that of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the House and the people might congratulate him and rest assured* that the administration of the railways was of a satisfactory character. But the conditions are very different. I do not believe that 
the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific would be satisfied with the manner in which that road was managed if the directorate laid before them a financial statement similar to that submitted by the Minister of Railways. I think they would require some information; I think they would press the directorate for fuller details than those which have been submitted to us. But when the Government refused to the House the other day the information of which it was in need, public sentiment was aroused; from one end of the country to the other newspapers friendly to the Government took up the question and intimated that such a condition should not prevail; that the Government should lay before the people, through the House of Commons, all information necessary to enable the legislators to find a remedy for the great evil which existed.
The right hon. gentleman has felt the pulse of public opinion. He says to-day: I am desirous that all information that is required shall be laid on the Table, but there is some information which we cannot give, which it would be against the national interest to ippke public; therefore we will appoint a committee and instruct it to make inquiries as to what information should be made available to the House. ,
This committee will not be instructed to call witnesses in respect to the management of the railway. The Minister of Justice, answering that point, says that they will. Well, paragraph 4 of the resolution says that the committee shall have the right to examine witnesses under oath, to send for persons, papers and records and to report from time to time. Sir, for an hon. gentleman who was several years on the bench and who is to-day Minister of Justice of Canada, I think his legal interpretation of the resolution is not to be commended. I am sure that the right hon. gentleman did not read the resolution aright. I am sure that he did not deliberately attempt to lead the House into error. But he did make an error. The reference as it reads on the Order Paper does not assign to the committee the duty of investigating the management of the Canadian National railways; they will be entitled to summon witnesses and call for papers, but only on such questions as may involve the determination of what information concerning the Canadian National railways and shipping should be furnished to the House. It is quite clear that the committee will not investigate the management of the Canadian National railways. It will simply report to the House what informa-

tion the House should seek, and as has been suggested by one of the ministers, if the actual information is to be obtained by the committee, a further step will have to be taken to that end by the grant of further powers. The method adopted by the Government is the surest method of avoiding what they want to avoid, the laying before Parliament of any information whatever. The committee will sit from time to time. Their investigation may be quite protracted. After they have sat for months; after the Government have passed all their Estimates and have advanced their legislation to a sufficient degree, the committee will lay on the Table a report advising the House to seek such and such information. Then a full discussion will take place in the House as to what further reference should be made to that committee, and after another protracted discussion the committee will be instructed to summon witnesses and obtain further information-but by that time prorogation will be at hand. I am afraid, therefore, that the information which we now require to enable us to form a sound judgment upon the question before the House will not be forthcoming during the present session. Sir, if the Government are absolutely sincere in their purpose they should not hesitate to accept the proposal of the leader of the Opposition. If they really want to lay the required information before the House during this session, now is the time to refer the matter to the proposed committee and to give them such powers as will enable them to collect the information. Under the method adopted by the Government, however, such a course will be impossible.
In discussing the resolution this afternoon, two words fell from the lips of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) which made clearer the real purpose underlying the resolution now before the House. He said: "Information was sought and we refused it; we take fully responsibility for doing so." But mark his following words. "But not to appear arbitrary we now propose this committee." What did the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) say? He said: "Before this committee we will bring the management who will say why the information should not be given." You have there in two words the whole principle underlying the policy of the Government in presenting that resolution. The Minister of Finance says: "We refuse the information; we take the responsibility of that refusal; but to save appearances, not
to appear arbitrary, we propose a committee to report on what information will be given." Then the Minister of Railways says: "We will bring the management of the Canadian National Railways before the committee to say why the information should not be given." Therefore, the committee, after it has concluded its work, will not be in a position to give such information to the House. Is it not a farce to treat such a serious matter in such a light way? If the committee were armed with full powers, it could judge what information the management should lay before the House. Why not entrust it with that work? As the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) said, we now instruct the committee to lay down the principles which will direct the operations of this House in respect of our Canadian National railways. If we can instruct a committee to lay down the principles which will direct our deliberations on such an important matter, why should we not entrust it with the work of collecting this information. This committee would be nonpartisan; it would be, I am sure, willing to -give to the Government all possible assistance and to collect such information as would enable the House to judge soundly and fairly the big questions which are at present involved. We knew that information was not forthcoming. The Minister of Railways, who is very busy at present-

The Minister is really a
marvel; he says that he can listen to two members at the same time. The minister told the House this afternoon that he had refused no information; that he had given an answer to all questions put. Why then should he object to give to the committee which will be entrusted with the work, whatever information that committee may require? But the minister was not accurate in his statement. There were put on the Order Paper quite a few questions which could not be answered. I put some questions that the minister did not answer, and

I am going to refer to them. But the greatest fault of the minister is not that he did not answer some questions; other questions he answered, but did not answer correctly. Of the two, I do not know which I prefer

his refusal to answer questions or the incorrectness of the answers that he gave. I put on the Order Paper this question hy which I was trying to obtain some information as to financial results per division:
1.	How many divisional points are there on the Government railways, and what are their names.
2.	In each of the said divisional points, during 1919 and 1920, what were gross receipts, the operating costs, and the surplus or deficit?
This was a pertinent question. The Minister of Finance this afternoon complained of the fact that we did not inquire as to the cause of the deficit. My question was in relation thereto; in an endeavour to find out where the deficit came from, I tried to obtain from the minister the results by divisions. In answer he said:
Railway accounting does not provide for earnings being shown for each divisional point.
My information was to the contrary. I went back to my informant, because I had seen financial statements so drawn, and my informant said: "Well, you were wrong in your question; a divisional point is purely and simply the chief place of a division." For instance, Fraserville is the chief place or divisional point of one division. The same is true of Riviere du Loup. Parent is a divisional point, and "the old foxy minister," my informant said, "took advantage of the form of your question, and he did not answer because you asked the financial statement for each divisional point. Put your question otherwise." I did so; I put my question in this way:
1.	How many divisions, or operating divisions,-
So that the matter might be quite clear to the minister.
-are there on the Canadian National railways, and what are their names?
2.	What was the result of operations for each of the said divisions in 1919 and 1920?
I was not more lucky. The answer was this:
Railway accounting does not provide for receipts, expenses, surplus or deficits being shown by divisions.
The minister is wrong. This is a falsehood. He did not wittingly answer so, hut I tell him it is a falsehood. He told me that the accounting was not kept by divisions; I tell him that it is-

speechtext: Order. I hope the hon. member will bear in mind some remarks from the Chair in the earlier stages of this debate. speechtext:
I have strictly adhered to
your ruling, Sir, as laid down at the opening of the discussion. I am following closely on the footsteps of the hon. minister, who said that he had refused no information, and am trying to make clear to the House that he has refused information in some cases, and in others given wrong information. Moreover, Sir, during the time you were replaced in the Chair, the hon. ministers notwithstanding your ruling, trespassed on many grounds on which we did not intend to enter. I would not like their statements to be spread broadcast throughout the country unchallenged, and what I am now trying to do is to challenge some of the statements of the hon. Minister of Railways. I shall try, however, to confine myself closely to one or two points.
There was, to my mind, a very serious condition of affairs in connection with the Canadian National railways in the northern part of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The condition was this. A number of railway conductors were operating trains in northern Quebec and northern Ontario, running through a country entirely settled with French-speaking people. Most of the passengers on these trains were lumber-jacks, going to and from the camps, and the farming population, most of whom could not speak English. The conductors could not speak French. Moreover, my information was that a considerable number of these conductors were drunk half the time.

In northern Ontario and
northern Quebec. I tried to obtain from the minister the names of these conductors, not to intimate to the House that they were drunkards, but so that our information might be complete and be of some assistance in discussing railway matters. From Quebec westward there are a number of stations which have no resident station agents. The result is that the passengers cannot purchase their tickets until they are on the train. Then one of two things happens. Either they pay the conductor on the train when he is drunk and he puts the money in his pocket, or he does not collect the fare at all. My information is that in two specific instances people boarded the Canadian National train at Cochrane and came down to Quebec without having their fares collected, and that in another case the conductor was drunk. So in order to obtain data which would be of some information to the House I put the following question on the Order Paper:
How many railway conductors are employed on the Government railways in Quebec?
The answer was 296. I asked also:
What are their names?
The answer was:
It is not considered to be in the public interest to publish the names of these conductors.
You see my point, Mr. Speaker. The minister said this afternoon that he had never refused any information, but here, in reply to my question, he says that it is not considered in the public interest to publish the names of these conductors. I say that it was in the public interest to know the names of these conductors so that we might find out by personal investigation, as no official information was forthcoming in the House, whether or not these conductors were reliable, and whether or not they should be dismissed. So on these two points it will be seen that the minister did not give full information to the House.
The deficits of which we now complain are due to several conditions. Some of these conditions apply generally to all railways. The general industrial and commercial conditions, for instance, affect the railways in the United States lust as they do the railways in Canada, and affect private-owned railways just as they do public-owned railways. Then such factors as increased pay-rolls, and increased cost of material, affect all railways, hut these conditions will re-adjust themselves when normal times return. Wages will be readjusted, as well as the cost of material,
but there is another cause of our deficits which it will be more difficult to remove.
I refer to the question of management, and this also involves the question of state ownership. This question was touched upon slightly this afternoon by the hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), who tried to justify state ownership. It was not our intention to discuss state ownership tonight, but I do not think we should allow his statements to go unchallenged. There are in this country friends of state ownership and there are also enemies of state ownership. The friends of state ownership belong mainly to the western provinces and to the province of Ontario. The other provinces are more conservative in this sense, and are opposed to state ownership. The friends of state ownership, Mr. Speaker, have no greater enemies than those who have introduced the principle into our legislation and those who were entrusted with the management of our national railways. If state ownership had been given a fair trial it is possible that we might have adjusted our national conditions to this new venture; but the management which has operated since the introduction of this policy will make, I think, for the prompt return to private ownership. It was quite easy to forecast that the present situation could not be avoided under the management that was provided for our national railways.
How did this situation come about? The Canadian Northern became insolvent and we took it over and nationalized it; and after that we entrusted the management of the Canadian National railways to the very group of men who had run the Canadian Northern into bankruptcy. They had not been able successfully to manage their own property, but when we took it from their hands as a private concern and assumed all their obligations, we put them in charge of the railways as public property. And that is a point intimately connected with the question now before the House. We want to have full and precise information as to how this group of men came to manage our railways in such a way as to create a deficit of $48,000,000 last year, $70,000,000 this year, and a predicted deficit of $100,000,000 next year. Mr. Speaker, the whole management has been altogether unwise, and no business man in this country could have followed a more foolish course. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) tells us that we shall have a committee before which we shall have the management of the national railways to

tell us why the information should not be forthcoming. Of course, they will try to convince Parliament that it is not in the public interest for them to submit any information. They have to hide the ways and means by which these deficits are created, and naturally they will try to prevent any information tending to throw light on the subject from getting to the public knowledge. We want the management of our Canadian National railways to give us, not, as the Minister of Railways says, reasons why information should not be forthcoming, but an account of their stewardship and reasons why they have not managed our railways to better advantage. We want them to give us some satisfactory explanation of the deficits that are making such inroads into the public treasury. All true Canadian patriots are greatly concerned over the state of affairs to-day.
