They are very much exercised over conditions, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the senseless laughter I hear on the other side. I see one hon.
9 p.m. member laughing. Well, the situation is too desperate for any serious-minded man to indulge in laughter.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: He does not sit on our side.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The people are worried to see our national heritage being squandered, and stolen, and wrecked, and yet an hon. member can find something in the situation to laugh at. Evidently the facts do not appeal to the hon. gentleman in their true light. However, he has given us the measure of his intelligence and his patriotism. Sir, those Canadians, whose ancestors settled in this country generations ago, and battled with adversity that future generations might have a country in which they could live happily and in prosperity, cannot look with equanimity upon the wreckage of the early hopes of their forefathers. It is painful to see our national heritage jeopardized in this way by the Government, who see nothing wrong in entrusting the management of our railways to the very men who ran their own property into bankruptcy, men who are evidently above Parliament and who can refuse this House the information of which it is badly in need. It is high time that we appointed a committee, not for the purposes of party politics but solely for the national welfare, who will work effectively

and devise some policy that might extricate the country from its present difficulties. It is useless appointing a committee - merely to report to Parliament as to what information should be sought and what should not. We must appoint a committee armed with powers and able to summon witnesses and conduct a thorough investigation, behind closed doors if necessary, but an investigation that will provide us something as a basis for intelligent discussion and sound legislation. In my opinion the resolution is purely and simply a sham; it is nothing but camouflage and will only serve to distract the attention of the House from the real issue under discussion. It will create a committee whose report will be purely and simply a "whitewash" for the Government, and will preclude this House from getting the information which it badly needs. On these grounds I cannot support the resolution of the Government, and I think that if they were sincere they would gladly welcome the amendment of the leader of the Opposition. For all the reasons I have given I am ready to support the amendment and to vote the resolution down.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I have been a strong advocate of the appointment of the proposed committee for some time, although I confess that the reference is not worded exactly as I would have worded it. At the same time it affords the committee an opportunity, especially under the fourth clause, to make a great many inquiries. The annual report of the Board of Management will be laid before the committee, and I am inclined to think that by the time the committee have inquired into its contents they will have gathered a great deal of information. I have no hesitation whatever in thinking that should the committee, when organized, find that the reference restricts their investigations in any way, and they ask the House to enlarge their powers, the House will be very glad to meet their wishes. Whether they will be able to formulate a report satisfactory to themselves will depend upon the information they bring out during the inquiry. I have no doubt whatever that the reference is quite wide enough to enable them to get all the information they require, at am rate to commence with. I am not in favour of appointing counsel for the committee or of bringing traction experts to testify. In the majority of cases traction experts, in my judgment, would talk over the heads of the committee. I take it that

the committee will consist of business men selected from both sides of the House, and it is the operation of the national railways that will form the subject of inquiry. The members of the committee will be perfectly competent, in my judgment, to elicit the necessary information without the guidance either of counsel or traction experts. Should this not prove to be the case it will be the easiest thing in the world for the committee to agree that they need legal and technical advice and upon a representation to that effect the House will, no doubt, comply with their wishes.
I have sat on a good many special committees and the experience gained in that way leads me to support the present proposition. Through the medium of a committee information can be obtained very promptly without consuming hours of talk. If the House itself were to undertake to probe the details of the management of the national system of railways, and were to spend an hour or two, or a whole afternoon, in discussing why a station master was dismissed, or why ties were not laid in certain spots at a certain length, or why the management did not buy coal from John Jones in place of Thomas Oliver, or similar questions, Parliament might just as well sit for the whole year, instead of for only a few months. For the reasons I have given I am very much in favour of a committee being appointed, and I am quite sure their deliberations will result in the presentation of information that will be very valuable, even if it does not reduce the deficit on the operations of this railway system, as I hope it will.
I agree with everything that has been said as to the desirability of carrying on the inquiry from a non-partisan standpoint, and I was sorry to hear one hon. member state this afternoon that the appointment of such a committee even under the powers given by the reference, would mean that there would be a majority and a minority report, ^rsonally, I do not think that observation should have been made. In my opinion predictions of that kind should not be indulged in. None of those who are chosen as members of the committee should be influenced by such a spirit as that, because it is useless for hon. gentlemen to become members of this committee if they are going to make up their minds in advance as to what conclusions they shall reach. In my opinion, those hon. gentlemen who are honoured with a seat upon the committee should go to their deliberations with open minds, they should
discuss any matters which may come before them in a quiet and businesslike way, and make their report to the House after due consideration. I hope that is the policy that will be followed in this case.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I am in favour of the amendment and intend to vote for it, my reason therefor being that I feel it is something that will appeal to the people of this country, whereas the resolution of the Prime Minister cannot appeal to any person who has made a study of the railway and shipping problem as it presents itself to-day in Canada. The resolution has, to my mind, been rendered ineffective at the very moment of its birth. No matter what conclusion is arrived at it is not going to give satisfaction, because it appears to me to be something which is made purely for the purpose of shelving the important question now before the House. For instance, the first clause of this resolution states that the proposed committee will inquire into:
What information as to operation of Canadian National railways and shipping as conducted by the Board of Directors and Management should, in the public interest, be brought down _in Parliament on Questions, Motion for Production of Papers, or otherwise.
What information should be brought down to Parliament? I ask myself how the people outside are going to view this highly important question. What information should be brought down to Parliament on "questions, motion for production of papers, or otherwise?" I venture to say that not one person outside really knows what that means. To parliamentarians, of course, it simply means that the Government is asking a committee of this House to tell them what they ought tt>
do. The Government practically abdicates its functions and asks a committee-the majority of whom will be from their side of the House-to tell them what they shall do. Well, Mr. Speaker, water never rises above its own level. How is it possible that this committee, the creatures of the Government, can tell the Government what information shall be brought down to Parliament "on question, motion for production of papers, or otherwise"? The second paragraph says:
When, by what method, and under what conditions, if any, should such information be given,-
"If any." That is simply placing a fence around the committee before any question is submitted to it at all. And I ask again



what the people outside the House will think of that. The third paragraph reads:
What system of auditing should he adopted, and what extent of detail should be given in the Annual Report.
I feel like saying, as did a celebrated character in Shakespeare, "A plague on both your houses." What does the public care about auditing and the extent of detail of the report? They will look at what is called the "demnition total." They will not care what system of auditing has been adopted. Then the fourth and final paragraph:
Whether and for what purposes the said committee should he continued, and that for the above purposes and for such other purposes as the committee deem in the public interest there be referred to said committee the Annual Report of the Board of Directors.
Just imagine! We have the annual report of the Board of Directors before us now, but we are still in Egyptian darkness with regard to the entire situation. Yet we expect that a committee which we are going to appoint-is going to study the annual report of the Board of Directors and tell us what we shall do! Well, my experience of the annual report of any board of directors is that usually it is a recital of what the board does not do rather than of what it does. We have the annual report of the Board of Directors here, we have a Government, at the head of which is one of the most astute and agile minds in the country, and we know something at least about auditing and details,-and yet this is what the committee are going to study! In my opinion we have wasted an entire day of valuable time at a considerable cost to this country, and we have arrived nowhere.
Now, this amendment which is proposed by the leader of the Opposition contains something constructive. It reads:
That such committee shall have power to inquire into all matters in any way relating to the railways owned or controlled by the Government of Canada whether under the direction of the Department of Railways and Canals or under any corporation in which the Government are stockholders, whether relating to the construction or operation, from the date of the appointment by the Government of the Board of Directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company down to the present time; and similarly to inquire into all matters in any way connected with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, either in respect of the construction or operation of the ships, and that such committee shall have power to send for papers, persons, and records, to engage counsel-

That appeals to me.
-and transportation experts, and to make such reports and recommendations from time to time as, in their judgment, wTill be calculated to promote the public interest.
Put these two documents side by side, the proposed resolution and the amendment, and ask yourself, Mr. Speaker, which will appeal to the man in the street, to the people outside-because, after all they are the people who pay the piper, and surely they have a right to call the tune. I venture to say that if any hon. member on the other side of the House were to back up this resolution on the hustings proposed by the Prime Minister and ask that it be preferred to the amendment, he would be considered a candidate for a lunatic asylum. There is no comparison between the two. One proposes to do something constructive, to get at the root of the trouble, to explain to the public what is the difficulty; and the other is a sterile resolution which, as far as I can judge, appears to have been drawn by the hon. Minister of Justice-I recognize his hand.
We are told, and told rather seriously, that it is not in the public interest that everything should be known in regard to the operation and management of these two enterprises. When a person is sick and goes to a physician, he tells the physician what it is that he is suffering from, and the physician then diagnoses his case and prescribes the remedy. But suppose the patient were to say to the physician, "I suffer from this, that and the other thing but I also suffer in another way, and I cannot tell you what it is because I feel that you may possibly lose confidence in me and not consider me to be such a gentleman as you thought me before, for telling you what I am suffering from." How is it possible, Mr. Speaker, to diagnose a case and prescribe the necessary medicine unless you know what the patient is suffering from? Yet our friends on the opposite side of the House tell us: "We will only let you have such information as in the public interest we can let you have." What is the public interest in this case? The public interest is the interest of the public in this country, the men who pay this $70,000,000 or $80,000,000 a year deficit, and who are going probably to have to pay $100,000,000 next year; they are the people who form the public, and they are interested in knowing all the facts. The- public interest, as I understand from this resolution, is that of the management of the national railways. Apparently it is feared that some information may come out which may not be favour-

able to the management; they are the people who want to save their skins.
Now, I challenge my hon. friends on the opposite side of the House to give me one instance of what they consider would be damaging to the public if it came out in the investigation before this committee. What is this insidious trouble that is preventing the Government from bringing it before the public? We are the public, we represent the public, and we say we are satisfied to know what it is all about. We want to know what the difficulty is. We care not at all about the interests of the management of the system; we want to know what it is that this line is suffering from which results in such enormous deficits every year. I challenge the Government again to tell me what possible item could there be which might not be in the public interest if it came out. My hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) says that the Canadian Pacific may copy our methods! As we say in French, C'est pour rire; or in English, it is to laugh. As my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) said toeday, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company copy the secrets of success, they never copy the secrets of failure. What is there in the Canadian National Railway system which if to-day given out to the public would enure to the advantage of the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other company or person?
When a person is suffering from the dread disease of tuberculosis, Mr. Speaker, the doctor prescribes sunshine and fresh air, and that is what you want here. We are suffering from hemorrhages at the rate of $70,000,000, and we want sunshine and fresh air to cure us. Nothing, Mr. Speaker, was ever accomplished in the way of a public enterprise by hole-in-the-corner methods. These gentlemen on the other side are merely temporary stewards of the affairs of this country; they are here today and to-morrow they will be elsewhere. But the people are here all the time, and they are demanding in no uncertain tones that a full investigation be made into the affairs of these enterprises, in order that they may ascertain whether it is possible to stop this ensanguination; whether it is possible to get these government lines on the proper track in the same way as other successful lines.
Will the Government tell me in what possible way we can be in a worse position than we are to-day? It is declared by those on the other side who are supposed to know that the public interest would not be served
if certain information was brought out. Well, even if it were brought out, would the result be the loss of more than seventy or eighty millions a year? Should we lose then ninety millions a year? I say that it would be well if we lost one hundred millions a year if the result would be to enable us to put a finger on the sore spot and obtain some relief from the situation.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar)-I do not see him in the House this evening-took high moral ground this afternoon. He spoke words of wisdom, and his manner of uttering them was such as a statesman would be supposed to employ in the delivering of weighty opinions. He told us that he had a complaint, not against the Government who were charged with the responsibility of the operation of these railways and who are the chief offenders in this matter, but against the leader of the Opposition. He complained that the leader of the Opposition had put before the House no constructive suggestion in regard to the operation of these two Government enterprises. Well, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that he should not have passed so lightly over the head of the Prime Minister, who, after all, is the most serious offender in this matter. How is it that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways threw themselves on the mercy of the country when in the House a few days ago they told us they were willing to receive suggestions from any and all sources in regard to the operation of these Government enterprises? Was that a constructive policy, Mr. Speaker? Why did the hon. member for Marquette not deem it necessary to advert to this so-called constructive policy on the part of the Government? Then, strange to relate, the hon. member passed over himself, the leader of a party which, though not yet great, is potentially great, a party which at least hopes to be great and hopes very shortly to be seated on the other side. That is a very noble ambition; I am sure that many of the people are of the opinion that anything would be better than the aggregation we have on the Government benches at the moment. Well, the hon. member for Marquette did not suggest any constructive policy. He did say a few weeks ago, when he was discussing this subject that the only solution of the problem now before the country was to revalue the assets of the national railways. That was the constructive policy which the Agrarian party put forward. Well, what is the use of revaluing this property? What purpose would be served? I venture to say that if

it were suggested that a provision for the revaluation of the property should be inserted in this resolution, the Prime Minister would not allow it to go in, on the ground that it is not in the public interest that a revaluation should be made. The only ostensible reason why the property should be revalued at the moment is that we might make it enticing to some party or syndicate who would went to purchase it on the basis of that revaluation. Does my hon. friend from Marquette want to sell out so soon to a private syndicate? It is only a few months since the whole of the aggregation sitting close to us-but not of us-were proclaiming in the loudest tones that the only salvation of this country was public ownership. Now the leader of their party states that he wants a revaluation of the lines. This is his constructive policy, and then he puts it up to the leader of the Opposition to declare the constructive policy of the Liberal party in this regard. Now, I have a great regard for the leader of the Opposition. I have followed him and I hope to follow him for some considerable time. But I am not prepared to say that he is a superman, and it would certainly require more than an ordinary human being to bring some order out of the chaos which at present prevails, at least until we have before us such facts and figures and such information as would be brought out by a committee operating as the leader of the Opposition suggests. "Are you guilty or not guilty?" asks the magistrate of a prisoner in the dock. The prisoner replied: "Well, how can I tell until I have heard the evidence?" That is the position in which we all find ourselves. We would like to hear the evidence; we would like to know something concerning this matter before we find the Government guilty, although we have very shrewd suspicions that they are guilty.
In 1916 I was one of the counsel employed in connection with the Meredith-Duff Commission appointed to inquire into matters affecting shell contracts with, which the names of several ministers of the Crown had been connected in some way. The matter was brought up in the House by Mr. Kyte, I believe, in a very strong speech. The Government decided, of course, that no investigation would be granted, but within a week or ten days, and after hearing what the country had to say, they retracted their steps and were glad indeed to grant a commission with the fullest powers of investigation. No question was raised about the public or private interest, al-

though it is to be borne in mind that we were investigating the matter of munitions, of shells, of explosives, in the midst of the war. We were obliged to bring before the commission of inquiry some matters the disclosure of which might have been considered at that time to be highly dangerous, in view of the fact that all this information was going abroad to the enemy. Information was brought out concerning the places at which these shells were being manufactured, the quantities that were being turned out, how they were being delivered across the ocean, the prices that were being paid for them, and various technical details in that connection,-all of which, it could have been said at that time, might furnish valuable information to the enemy. But in view of the fact that the public were demanding this investigation and that the honour of certain members of Parliament was at stake, the fullest and freest investigation was made and a report was submitted accordingly. Now, if during war time we were able to go into such a delicate matter as that to which I have referred, why should information not be given to the House and to the country in regard to the important and momentous question which we are now considering? I venture to say that if a plebiscite were taken on the question whether this information should be given or withheld because its disclosures is not in the public interest, by ninety-nine to one the people of this country would declare that they wanted information of the fullest character no matter what the result would be. They would want us to hew to the line no matter where the chips were to fly. It is not at all surprising, therefore, that we should insist upon the amendment proposed by the leader of the Opposition and refuse to accept the proposal put forward by the Government.
It is evident-and the extent to which this is true is a source of surprise to me- that hon. gentlemen on the other side will follow blindly the lead of the Prime Minister on this question and, as is most probable, vote accordingly. The matter which we are discussing is one of the most important which has come before the country for some considerable time. Probably they feel that they have very little to lose. "Those whom the Gods wish to destroy, they first drive mad," and my hon. friends feel that, as long as they last and as long as they occupy the Government benches, they will hang together with their friends on the Canadian National Railway. They alone are the people interested in not disclosing

information. They alone are attempting to burk this inquiry before it is started.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDIE (West Calgary) :
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion in connection with this resolution has gone pretty far afield, and it has been presented to the House in different forms on many occasions since the opening of the session. While I do not purpose discussing in detail many of the matters which have been referred to, I must ask the indulgence of the House to-night while I refer to one or two matters.
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in his endeavours to bring these matters before the public, has no doubt served a public purpose, and the various discussions which have taken place have been of the utmost importance in that they have impressed upon the people of this country the financial condition in connection with the national railways which are operated by this Government. If the people generally throughout the length and breadth of this land have followed these discussions, there can be hardly a man or a woman in Canada who does not recognize the fact that government operation and government control of railways have resulted in a heavy deficit. Notwithstanding the fact that that information came to the public in connection with the operation in 1919, when there was a deficit of some $45,000,000, I do not believe that there was spread over this country the gloom which hon. members of the Opposition would lead us to believe there was, because, notwithstanding the fact that we had a deficit then this Government has been besieged with requests from every part of the Dominion to carry on to a greater extent public works which were commenced or which were delayed during the war. Not later than January of this year there met in the city of Edmonton the United Farmers of Alberta, and notwithstanding the "blue ruin" which they, the Opposition, pointed out, they have submitted to the Dominion Government a whole series of resolutions in connection with railway construction, insisting and urging the Government still to carry forward with the utmost speed the policy which they have carried on in the past in connection with railway construction. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) must have received a copy of these resolutions and, if so, he will know that the very first thing which they enacted by resolution was:
That, in the opinion of this Union, No. 1 U.F.A., the ti-me has arivefl when, for the best interests of Canada, her railways should be nationalised over all lines.
As regards respect and admiration for the Canadian Pacific railway, the hon. member for Marquette expressed himself clearly in the words of adulation and praise which he uttered in this House this afternoon. The Canadian Pacific railway, as he stated, is a railway which has the best management and operating staff of any railway in the world. With this I quite agree, and would even go farther. The Canadian Pacific railway was a railway which, from the very inception of the road, started its management and operation with such an eminent and capable man as Lord Mount Stephen; it has always maintained this high standard in the selection of its officials and it has attained greater degrees of excellence in its management and operation than has ever been attained by any other railway in this country. But while the hon. member for Marquette took great care this afternoon to express to the House his views in relation to the Canadian Pacific railway he stopped short of the real vital question, with which the people of Canada are concerned. Members of the House directly opposite us [DOT] say that they are opposed to the nationalization and government operation and control of railways. The hon. member for Marquette, who stands up in this House and lauds the management of the Canadian Pacific railway and points out that it Is without a peer in this country, was by that same convention which passed that resolution, approving of the immediate nationalization of all railways, approved as leader of the Agrarian party in the Dominion of Canada. Let him state in this House whether or not he, as leader of the Agrarian party, is in favour of the immediate nationalization of the Canadian Pacific railway and let him make his position clear to the people. Personally, I have no hesitation	whatever in expressing my
views	in regard to that road.
This Government should make its decision absolutely clear that it has no intention to undertake in any way, shape or form the nationalization of the Canadian Pacific railway, but that it is its opinion that we should keep our hands off one of the best organized, best administered and best managed railway corporations in the world. We shall be pleased to have the leader of the Agrarian party state clearly, irrespective of the views of the party which he leads throughout Western Canada, what his views are in connection with that problem.
We have heard a great deal about this deficiency in connection with the operation

and management of the Canadian National railways; but the proper comparison has never been made, and I trust that it will be made at some time before the close of this session of Parliament. Hon. members opposite have taken a deficit of $45,000,000 last year and a deficit of some $70,000,000 this year, and they say that, because there was a deficit in each of those two years and because there probably will be a deficit next year, this country is facing blue ruin, because it has taken over the operation of the national railways. If they wish to be fair in that question, their comparison should be made, not with the Canadian Pacific as it exists at the present time, but with the Canadian Pacific when, some thirty or forty years ago, it was a pioneer railway in this country. We all recall that, when that great organization, of which we are all now so proud and which we lend our voice in this House to praise, was passing through pioneer days in the Dominion of Canada, insolvency faced it, even though under private management, and if the Dominion Government had not come to the aid of that corporation, insolvency would have been its state. There is not in the Dominion of Canada a single railway corporation which has not received aid from the treasury of the Dominion Government, and the time came, in connection with the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk railway, for us to say whether or not we should still continue giving further aid to those roads, or whether we should take and appropriate them to the Dominion of Canada and spend our money on that which is our property.
A great deal has been said back and forth about the question of government ownership; but the question of government ownership in connection with railways has never come properly and fairly before the House. Government ownership was not the result of the expression of the will of the people; it was not the result of any overwhelming desire on their part that these roads should be taken over; but we found ourselves in a position that we must take these roads over in order to protect the investment of the country.
On a former occasion, when this matter was being discussed, we had the privilege of hearing the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) deliver in this House an address in which he said that the West had been practically purchased by the Dominion; that Western Canada was the vassal of eastern capital; that they were supporting us and that the Dominion treasury wras

being bled for those people. I want to tell the hon. member for Dorchester that Western Canada is no vassal of eastern capital; that Western Canada is not dependent upon Eastern Canada for support; but that Western Canada is delighted to receive the investment of eastern capital, and eastern capitalists are pleased to invest their funds in the West, because they feel that there is no other part of the whole Dominion and very few parts in the world where they can receive better returns for the money they invest than Western Canada.
So far as the railway problem in Western Canada is concerned, they go on to say that these railways have been built for the development of Western Canada, and that as a result we have these deficits growing larger from year to year, and they will grow still larger in the future. But, Mr. Speaker, if at the time these Transcontinental lines were constructed a safe and sane policy had been carried out by the Government under the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, if he had followed the policy which was advocated by the Hon. Andrew G, Blair and had refused to come to the assistance of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, refused to embark upon the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental, we would be absolutely freed from the position in which we find ourselves to-day. If they had confined themselves, as they started out to do, to the construction of railway lines in the Prairie Provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, I believe that under present conditions every foot of railway in the Dominion of Canada would be self-supr porting, and that there would be no charge against the public treasury for maintenance, operation, or overhead charges in connection with any of the roads. Throughout the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba we must originate practically all the freight which must take care of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Transcontinental and the Canadian National. That is the burden which was unfairly and unjustly imposed on the West. Those roads go through the wilderness of northern Ontario, through the wilderness of Quebec, and through part of the wilderness of the province of New Brunswick. They serve these three eastern provinces, yet hon. gentlemen will get up in this House and charge the deficit on these roads to the three Prairie Provinces, when the roads are their own children, and run through their own territory. I submit that these deficits are not chargeable to the West, but to the three

older provinces, from which came the majority who forced upon the Government the programme which compelled them to build these lines as a'matter of political patronage. But these matters will be gone into at some other time at great length. I just wish to say now that there is not one private road in the United States, I believe, but what has passed through the bankruptcy court, or at all events very few. So far as deficits and the matter of insolvency are concerned, the position which we have in Canada to-day corresponds exactly with that which existed in the United States. I believe that the Government did its duty when it took over the responsibility of the administration of these roads.
I wish to say a few words in connection with the resolution of the Prime Minister which is now before the House. Great exception has been taken to it, and an amendment has been moved by the leader af the Opposition. I wish to point out to the leader of the Opposition the inconsistency of the stand which he as a party leader in this House takes in connection with his amendment. On March 15, we were discussing, at the instance of the leader of the Opposition, the question of the public accounts of this country and he complained bitterly on that occasion that only three volumes of the Auditor General's report had been placed before the House, and that they could not investigate the financial condition of the country until they had the fourth volume. He says, on page 946 of Hansard:	.
Mr. Speaker, before this motion carries I should like to point out to the Government the impossibility of this House proceeding intelligently with a consideration of the Estimates until it has before it the full report of the Auditor General.
He goes on:
A part of that machinery is the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act which has a special provision respecting the presentation to Parliament of the Auditor General's Report.
Then on page 949 he says:
That is the point of which we are complaining at the moment. There is not an opportunity to intelligently discuss these Estimates until we have in its completed form the Auditor General's report of the preceding fiscal year, and until we have several other reports which have already been asked for, and concerning which we can get no definite information from the Government. I think, Sir, that until we get a definite assurance from the Government that we are going to have a proper opportunity of discussing the Estimates with reports in their complete and full form we would not he justified in proceeding at the present moment with the consideration of any portion of those Estimates.
What is his position briefly? He says we cannot have a meeting of the Public Accounts Committee because only three volumes of the Auditor General's Report have been laid upon the Table and we have not got the fourth. We will assume for the purposes of argument that his reasoning on that occasion was just. What do we find his position to be at the present time? Has he any details of the operation of the Canadian National railways? Have there been submitted to the Auditor General or to any one else the detailed accounts of the business of those railways? Why, Sir, that is just what they have been complaining of in this House, complaining that they have not received those details. Yet the hon. gentleman stands up in his place in this House, and notwithstanding the fact that only a short time ago he said, we must have all the details before the committee can intelligently discuss this matter, he says now, let us have a committee to go into all the accounts of the Canadian National railways, when he has not before him one vestige, not one detail, he says, except the report which was laid on the Table. Is he sincere when he says that in the interests of the people of Canada we must investigate the transactions of the Canadian National railways? What is the genius of his mind which on one occasion says, I cannot examine without facts and figures, and on the other occasion says, I do not need anything before me, all I want is the committee? Does this House want any further proof that his amendment means simply and purely one of two things? It means either a fishing excursion in which he wishes to get a little group of men around the table and then produce from his vest pocket or from the vest pocket of some other hon. member, some bit of gossip which he may have picked up on the street and then say to the witness, Tell us all about that. Can it be that that which he has alleged to be the policy of the Government, that which he has so consistently denounced in this House, in alleging the denial on the part of the Government of information to the House of Commons, is the proper course to pursue, or does he wish to lead the people to believe that this House is suppressing information which should be given out? Mr. Speaker, whichever one of these alternatives he accepts, I submit that neither of them should justify this House in supporting the amendment which he has introduced. As between the resolution and the amendment the difference is this: The hon. the Prime Minister says

that this is something new in the history and development of this country, that the operation of transcontinental railways was never before contemplated and that we want instructions. All that the resolution asks is for the committee to determine whether information shall be given, when that information shall be given, and what shall happen in connection with the auditing of the accounts. The leader of the Opposition says, we must have all the information. His amendment is definite, it is conclusive. Mr. Speaker, I submit that this House should appoint that committee to consider the question of whether or not the information should be given. We should call before that committee representatives of the management of the road, in order that they may point out to us the difficulty there would be in making the whole thing public. We should also call before that committee representatives ' the men, in order that they may lay their views before the committee as to what the effects of this publicity would be. These questions should be considered by the committee and reported on to the House.
As to the question of auditing, if my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition wishes to accomplish the purpose which he has in view, it should be accomplished only in connection with the Audit Act and the Consolidated, Revenue Act of this country. There should appear in the public accounts every single dollar of expenditure in connection with that road, and the accounts should be audited and approved by the Auditor General and submitted to the House. Is either of these courses wise? Do we want to allow a committee of this House to investigate every transaction in connection with the railways? Why, a man out in British Columbia may have a team of horses killed and the board may determine what compensation he shall receive; but he may be dissatisfied and he immediately communicates with the member of Parliament representing his constituency qnd that member brings the matter up before the committee. Under such circumstances the whole session of Parliament might be taken up in determining whether or not such people were properly compensated or not. Do you want these questions investigated by that committee? Do you want the committee to go into such matters as, for instance, the removal of a roundhouse at a certain place, the discharge of one of the section hands, the question of a conductor who is drunk on duty or negligent in his duty, the expropriation of a right-of-way,
[Hr. Tweedie.]
and so forth? Do you want every single question of this nature brought before the committee?
I quite agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. La-fortune) in his reference to the hon. mem-[DOT] ber for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). The hon. member for Marquette says that we do not want all these things to be gone into, and that is the reason why he opposes bringing down the papers and documents. He does not want these matters discussed in the House. But the hon. member must know that if the committee were given the discretion to consider whatever questions they saw fit, every single one of these things could be discussed by the committee and the House; so that when he advocates a wide open door it simply means the institution of a political campaign in connection with the administration of the railways. The hon. member for Marquette said he did not believe that all these things should be inquired into but that we should inquire into questions of policy. Did he move any amendment? He made no suggestion, so that his position is simply this, that we should throw the door wide open, carry all our political quarrels into the committee on railways, and simply debauch the administration of the railways of this country. I know of no rock which is more likely to wreck the ship of government control in connection with our railways than permitting the House of Commons to get its hand on the adjustment of these various matters. The effect of such a policy would be to destroy the authority of the management and of the officers of the roads. They might make a decision in some matter and the party concerned would simply say:
"Your decision is not final; I 10 p.m. have another court of appeal.
I can go to my representative and he will bring the matter before the Railway Committee of the House." Now, Mr. Speaker, we are at a crisis in connection with the administration of our-railways, and this House must determine once and for all whether or not it is going to tolerate any committee that will inquire into private differences and private arrangements, and all these minor transactions in the operation and management of the railways. I believe that the constitution of the railway employees now is such that, while the management might possibly not object to interference of this kind, the men themselves would undoubtedly oppose it very strenuously, because, having got any

matter in contention adjusted with the management of the railways, they would not want this or any other government to intervene. Nothing fairer can be suggested to the House than the resolution of the Prime Minister that this matter should go to a committee for consideration as to what the extent of inquiry shall be, and the House could then either adopt or reject the report of that committee and perhaps establish a final policy for all time.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
To
paraphrase the language of a British statesman of about a century ago, we are to-day like fishermen sitting on an empty chest by a bottomless pool of deficiencies seeking for a method of management. Our trouble to-day is that we have endeavoured to engraft upon the methods and practices of responsible government the advantages of corporate management, and the fact that the Government has had to bring down this request for a committee is evidence that that graft has not been a successful one. And now we are asked to examine it and decide what is to be done in the matter. As I have sat listening to the debate to-day, I have been trying to imagine this concern as a body of shareholders considering the report of their directors upon a deficit in the operations of the company. Now, why have we not been able to examine the situation just as such directors would? The reason is quite plain. Here we are playing a bigger game than that played by the directors of any company; we are playing a different game. These deficits on shipping and railways are after all but one-sixth of the whole field of management that comes under our control. Consequently, every question which may come up in relation to this subject, if it can throw discredit upon the government of the day, is a matter of public importance to the Opposition. Not only is that true of the existing House, but it would be well for us to keep in mind that some day there will come a change in the government of the country and then what is now set up as precedent may continue to operate to the grave disadvantage of the country in general and of this enterprise in particular. In examining the resolution of the Prime Minister, it seems to me that, were it not for the many speeches that have been made as limiting the sense and scope of the inquiry, the wording of the first sentence would carry us far on the road towards what the amendment asks for:
(1) What information as to operation of Canadian National Railways and Shipping as conducted by the Board of Directors and Management should, in the public interest, be brought down in Parliament on Question, Motion for Production of Papers, or otherwise.
Now, two or more years ago when we considered this matter the case was hypothetical. We had not then the reports of the company for examination; we had not the record of government ownership. Today we have that record, and in my opinion the country will absolve us from any charge of party politics and will say that we have been wise if, in view of deficits amounting to more than $120,000,000 in two years, we turn the whole management upside down, shake it apart and see what has happened. I cannot see that it is wise to approach this question in any other way, and taken in its widest sense and devoid of the interpretations that have been put upon it by Government speakers, that is what that first sentence means. How can you judge of the conduct of the Board unless you go into all matters with which they have had to do?
Now there are one or two things that cause grave discredit to the Government, or at any rate to the management of the railways, at the present time. A gentleman at one time sat in this House whom the Prime Minister of that day read out of the party who to-day is a purchasing agent for the national railways in the city of Chicago. If such things can happen it points directly to some political connection between the management of the railways and the party of which he was a member. In consequence I take it that we have to go the whole road in connection with this examination; and if it were not, as I say again, for the speeches which have been made in limitation of this interpretation I would take that first sentence to mean that very thing. Again, as was pointed out, I think, by the Minister of Justice, in the fourth clause of the resolution there are words going to the same extent:

and for such other purposes as the committee deem in the public interest there be referred to said committee the Annual Report of the Board of Directors and that the said committee have power to examine witnesses-
And so forth. But with the interpretations which have been put upon the report, and no answer having been made to the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) who spoke a moment or two ago asking for instances of what should be exempted from examination by this committee, I am inclined to believe that the Government do mean something by their

language other than what I would take the broad meaning of the resolution to be. Now, finally, I would say this with regard to the matter. It could all be fixed with the addition of perhaps a dozen words if the resolution read:
That a Select Standing Committee on National Railways and Shipping be appointed for the present session and be instructed to enquire into all matters relating to Government Shipping and Railways, and to report upon the following questions-
And so forth. Then I would be entirely content with the reference. We are playing a bigger game here-and the country realizes the fact-than merely managing a railway; we are managing a country, and the expenditures for this railway system represent only a sixth part of this year's estimates of expenditures. That being the case we cannot examine the situation apart from the political position, and the result is that we have apparent limitations put upon the meaning of this reference. Now, if the matter could be read in the light that I have suggested, I would support the resolution. But just as I stand at present I shall have to vote for the amendment, although I shall never consider it as a precedent for the House going, every year and on every possible occasion, into the management of these railways. But with the experience that we have had I think we must now investigate the management in order to satisfy the country. Should the Government accept the interpretation of their resolution which I have suggested I would be pleased indeed to vote for their commitment and a confining of the investigation to those purposes which, in the long run, must be the purposes sought by the House.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Having sat through most of the afternoon and evening listening, as intently as I might, to the remarks that have,been made on the resolution and amendment before the House, I have been forced to the conclusion that many of the hon. members who have spoken, and have taken the position that they have with regard to each proposition, were either not in the House when the Prime Minister made his statement in relation to the scope of the inquiry he suggested the committee should have, or else they have not read the amendment proposed by the leader of the Opposition. In addition to the four clauses specifically set out in the motion, the Prime Minister stated that he was willing to accept an amendment that would provide that the commit-

tee might inquire into what was the best system of management for the Canadian National railways-into the whole question of the general policy of the Government in relation to the management and operation of these railways. The Prime Minister stated definitely that if the resolution did not now provide that, he was willing to accept an amendment that would make it just that wide-that is that a committee of the House-let me repeat it- might inquire into the whole question of policy in relation to the management and operation of the Canadian National railways. The amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition sets out, not that the policy shall be inquired into, not that we shall determine whether we have decided on the correct management of the Canadian National railways, but that every detail of the management of the Canadian National railways must be investigated by this committee.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I am sorry to be
forced to disagree with my hon. friend, but if the amendment means anything it means that the committee would be appointed for the purpose I have indicated. If the committee does not carry out the purpose for which it is appointed then we had better not appoint a committee at all. The terms of the amendment are that the committee is to be appointed to inquire into all matters in connection with the operation of the Canadian National railways. -Now, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) spoke in relation to this matter, and in the first part of his speech he laid down a perfectly sound policy. I would ask that hon. gentleman particularly to pay attention to what I say for I think we are very largely in agreement. He laid down the perfectly sound policy that if we are ever going to have successful management of government-owned railways we must keep them clear of political influence; if we are ever going to be able to go out and get the right class of men to manage and operate these railways we have to place that confidence in them that will enable them to feel that we are going to let them do their work just as if they were employed by a private corporation. These were not his words, but I think he will agree that I have given a fair interpretation of what he said. Now he immediately turned round and followed that up by saying that while you cannot expect to bring these men into a situation that would make it possible for their acts as operating officers to be the subject of debate across the floor of this House, nevertheless, we should appoint a committee of Parliament who will have power to inquire into every matter in connection with the details of the operation of the Canadian National railways. Again, I think that is a fair statement of the position taken by the hon. gentleman. Now that is where the fundamental difference occurs between the proposals of the Prime Minister, and the proposals set forth by the leader of the Opposition. The first clause provides, that a committee shall be appointed to inquire into how far it is wise for Parliament to go in delving
into the details of operation of the Canadian National railways. That is what it means, to determine how far it is wise for us to go if we are to have successful management of our railways. The second clause is to ascertain by what method this information shall be given to the House and to the public. The third is to determine what system of auditing shall be adopted. The fourth, the broad clause, provides for referring the annual report of the board of directors to the committee, that they may inquire into it. And, finally, the Prime Minister says: If this is not sufficiently wide, we are ready to accept an amendment that will make it possible for the committee to inquire into what _ lines of policy may be followed in developing a better system for the management of the Canadian National railways.
I should like to submit one or two questions in relation to inquiring into the details of operation, because I submit that right there is the rock on which Government ownership is going to wreck itself, if it wrecks itself at all. We must either have management of the Government-owned railways independent of politics of we can.-not operate such railways successfully. If you open the door, as being suggested, to inquire into every detail of operation of these railways, how are you going to keep that operation free from politics?
When this committee meets and starts to inquire into this question in detail, and some point arises such as has been referred to in this and in previous debates-as to why one station has one agent and another two agents; as to why a section foreman was dismissed on some part of the line; as to why there are two trains running where somebody thinks there should only be one; as to why ties were purchased from one man and rails from another, and so on-in connection with the operation of these lines all over the country, who are we going to ask for detailed information? I submit that the very first man the committee would appeal to would be the president of the Canadian National railways. He would be brought before that committee to answer these questions. But what information would he be able give to the committee? He would say at once, " I know nothing whatever about any of these matters, and I am not in a position to answer your questions. You will have to bring such and such an officer who is in charge of that particular work in the department." And before you get through with the investigation you will have the

whole operating staff herein Ottawa answering questions, and then the Parliamentary committee would not know anything more about the operation of the railways than they did before, simply because they are not competent to pass judgment on matters of operation. That is the situation. The whole discussion would seem to indicate that it is in the minds of some hon. members that some one individual somewhere can be brougnt here and by being asked a series of questions can give to the House all this detailed information. Does anyone suggest that the president of the Canadian National railways is in personal contact with all of the diverse activities in connection with operation? In the first place, the system is divided into two parts, the eastern and the western, each with its general manager. These are the next executive officers we would bring here. The eastern lines are divided into a certain number of grand divisions or districts, and those in turn are divided into sub-districts. All the general superintendents or assistant general managers of these divisions would be the next group of men we would bring here. It is needless to labour the point further. Anyone who has any appreciation of a business of that character will see at once that to embark on such an investigation would not only lead the committee and Parliament into a hopeless maze, but would create a situation that would make it impossible for the Canadian people to get men to undertake the management and operation of their railways.
We must all admit that we are faced with a difficult situation, and that it is not easy to determine just where we must begin and where we must end in connection with how far Parliament can go in respect to these matters. It may be that this committee can serve a useful purpose in so far as getting some light with regard to how much detailed information Parliament may secure and (how much it is unwise for it to expect to secure. But let we repeat, that if there is a man in this House who expects that Canada is going to develop a system of publicly-owned railways efficiently operated, and that the officers of such railways are going to be dragged before parliamentary committees to explain why they did this or that particular thing in connection with details of operation, you may make up your minds once for all that our Canadian National railways instead of becoming a success will eventually bankrupt the country. You can never operate under those conditions.

The hon. member for Lotbiniere, Mr. Vien) in speaking on this subject indicated what is in the minds at least of some hon. members in regard to all these questions of detail when he said that there were 208 -I think that was the number; perhaps it was 228-conductors on a certain section of the Canadian National railways and they were going out on their trains in a state of intoxication, that they were stealing the public money, either not collecting it or putting it in their pockets, and so on, and the desire of the hon. member and of others who are supporting the position he takes was that the names of those conductors should be brought before the House of Commons for debate in order that we might dismiss them if found delinquent. Well, if that is the function of Parliament in connection with the operation of the Canadian National railways, the best thing we can do is to dismiss the officers whom we now have endeavouring to operate these railways. How long does any hon. member expect you would keep a self-respecting superintendent or general superintendent if the House of Commons is going to bring his employees before it and determine whether he is maintaining proper discipline or not? And yet that is what is stated on the floor of this House that we should have an investigating committee for, in order that information of that character should be secured and we should dismiss employees.'

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Turn out the bosses.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The question was asked, what is there in connection with the operation of the Canadian National railways that in the public interest cannot or should not be given. The answer to-that can simply be summed up in this way. If there is going to be successful government ownership of railways there must be independent management. I am ' not for one moment saying that the present management is all that it should be. It may be wholly wrong. When the general : question of what has already taken place and the position we at present find ourselves in comes up for debate, I may take advantage of the opportunity and say something with regard to that.
The principle, nevertheless, is this: so long as this managing body is retained, and until Parliament determines that it no longer has our confidence, we cannot ask it to appear before a committee of the

House or before the House itself and answer questions with regard to details of operation and management. I am inclined to think, knowing, as I do, some of the junior officers of the Canadian National railways, that the very moment you asked them to do that they would hand in their resignation. The hon. member for Marquette, I am sure, would say they would not be self-respecting men, not men with the capacity to do the work we expect of them, if they took any other position.
Is this proposed committee to sit in camera, as has been suggested? Has the House of Commons authority to appoint a committee to go off into some room, lock the doors, examine witnesses and obtain a lot of information and then determine what part of it shall be furnished to the House? Every single item of evidence taken by any such committee is the property not of the committee itself but of the House of Commons. The whole report and the evidence upon which it is founded will be the subject of debate in the House; every particle of detailed information will be threshed out here. Officers will be attacked, as was suggested this afternoon, with regard to matters concerning which they cannot defend themselves, and attacked, too, by men who know nothing about the subjects with which they deal. There is only one way out of this difficulty; accept the proposal of the Prime Minister. If this resolution is not wide enough, make it sufficiently wide so that the committee may inquire into the whole question of the management of the Canadian National railways. The question whether or not we have a proper system of management is a proper one for a parliamentary committee to inquire into, and is a proper subject for this House to debate. There are genuine differences of opinion on the question whether we are employing the best system of management. Here is exactly the difference between the resolution proposed by the Prime Minister and the amendment of the leader of the Opposition: one involves the question of principles, the other a question of details. If we want to set the principles to one side and go into the details; if we want to inquire how many section-men are working at a certain point; how many telegraph operators there are at certain stations; how many ties were laid in certain mileages-if we want all these things, then let us vote for the amendment. But if we want to inquire into the principles underlying the whole question of the government ownership and operation of these railways, let us adopt the resolution proposed by the Prime Minister. Personally,
I have no difficulty whatever in making up my mind on this point. I have contended ever since I have been in the House -not as an arden advocate of public ownership of railways, but as one who has had some slight connection with the operation of railways-that you will never operate successfully a publicly-owned railway or any other kind of railway so long as it is subject to political interference and political influence. That is what is contemplated in the amendment proposed by the hon. leader of the Opposition, and for that reason I will vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few remarks to make in support of the amendment of the leader of the Opposition purporting to enlarge the scope of the committee which is to inquire into matters affecting the operation of the Canadian National railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
In my humble opinion there is only one point to consider, and it is this: who are the proprietors of the Canadian National railways and the Canadian merchant marine? Are the proprietors entitled to information with regard to the management of these Government enterprises? That is the only question to be decided, the only question before the House. The management of our railways issue a report showing a deficit of $70,000,000 this years-the deficit last year was $49,000,000-and ask for a vote of $165,000,000. Surely we have the right to inquire into the circumstances which are responsible for this condition. Surely the information should be laid before the House in order that we may be able to ascertain the cause of these large deficits and endeavour, to the best of our ability, to remove that cause.
Let me illustrate my thought. If the Canadian national railways or the Canadian merchant marine were a private corporation in which you, Mr. Speaker, were a shareholder, and if the management brought down a report showing a deficit of $70,000,000 for the operations of last year and asking for a fresh budget of $165,000,000, surely it would be your right to have all the details and all the information made available in order that they might be examined and considered. You would ask for instance, what the company were paying for locomotives and for various kinds of equipment; what amount was paid out by way of salaries to the different employees of the company; how many em-

Would my hon. friend
allow me to.ask him a question? What does my hon. friend estimate the cost of operation of a 10,000 ton ship per month?

respect for my hon. friend who has just asked me a question, but not at all times. I am always delighted to answer any questions of his when he is serious, but I am sorry that he is not so to night.
