subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I should like to interject a few imperfect remarks into this debate. When one speaks of railway matters in this country, one might as well make up his mind that he is speaking of the very life of Canada, for there is no use disguising the fact that the solvency of Canada is very gravely challenged to-day by the present railway situation. I would agree to a committee being appointed with full powers to look into the railway situation and get all the information, but I am not in favour of a committee that will only ask for information that it will not get. If that is to be the bright feature from which Canadian democracy is to draw solace, I am not in favour of a committee of that kind.
When the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) submitted his annual statement on March 17, I felt a little pity for him, because he had the inglorious task of disclosing to the House another deficit on the year's operations of $70,000,000. But is that $70,000,000 the actual deficit? It is because I want to make sure that I favour the appointment of a committee with full powers to inquire and ascertain just what the deficit is. If the minister were in the House to-night, I would challenge him, as I did at the second session of 1919, when this House was sitting in the Victoria Museum, to deny that the deficit, this year instead of being $70,000,000, is nearer

$132,000,000. What can a committee do that has no powers at all? Can it change the capital liabilities of the different lines? Can it change the fixed annual charges? Not at all. I would also like to see a committee appointed that would inquire into the management, I think that is absolutely necessary. After all, Mr. Speaker, I think the great fault in the National railway system is the centralization of the management in the city of Toronto. I grant you that Toronto is a beautiful city; but it is also a peculiar city. It is endowed with many gifts, I grant, but it has a fatal defect. It is an intellectual city, a cultured city, a hospitable city. In matters literary, and in matters military, Toronto can always be depended upon to use discernment, but in matters political the vision of Toronto has always been distorted. We have the proof of that in connection with railway matters. It has always been a failure, and always will be.
If we had a committee with full powers to inquire into railway matters, Mr. Speaker, it would find out that on the Intercolonial, for instance, we have absolutely no modern bookkeeping methods. The Intercolonial is divided into three divisions- from Montreal to Mont Joli, from Mont Joli to Moncton, and from Moncton to Sydney and Halifax. Last year the Intercolonial had a $5,000,000 deficit, but yet the division from Montreal to Mont Joli had a $2,000,000 surplus. This year the very same thing is repeated. There is almost a $2,000,000 surplus on the division from Montreal to Mont Joli.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Is Bellechasse in that division?

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Yes, it is. Then I would point out that the superintendent of that division is handicapped in having always to await orders from Toronto. His name is Mr. E. L. Desjardins, and the general superintendent is Mr. J. E. Mora-zain. I can commend these men to the minister. They are the only two who are showing results on the Intercolonial Railway, and I think the minister would do well to get a few more French-Canadians of their calibre as railway men. All the train despatching orders for the division come from Toronto. From Chaudiere to my parish it is only 18 miles, and you cannot send a train out unless the locomotive hauls a certain amount of tonnage. Well, during the winter, when it is 10 or 15 below zero, a locomotive with a load of 60 cars

cannot clear the sidings, and to accommodate such trains it would be well to lengthen the sidings. It takes 8 hours to make that 18 mile run, with such tonnage, and time and a half to go to the end of the run. If this matter were inquired into I am sure that it would result in a great deal of money being saved in demurrage. I do not wish to criticize the increase in rates that has been granted by the Railway Commission, except to say that they did not use discretion in granting increases on commodities that could not stand the increase, such as brick and lumber. These increased rates have paralized the building industry. That is another matter that the committee might well look into.
The people of this country are called upon to pay an appalling amount to make good the losses on these railways, and they might as well open their eyes to the situation. Mr. Speaker, the burden imposed upon the public treasury by the mismanagement of the national railways cannot be characterized in fitting terms. War expenditures have accustomed the public to fabulous sums, but the figures in connection with the railway situation cannot be mitigated by familiarity with reckless expenditure. The deficit in 1919 totalled some $48,000,000; this year it is stated to be $70,000,000, but I contend that it is nearer $133,000,000. The people, I say, might just as well realize that this great system of railways is nothing but an old cripple which they have taken on their backs. Last year when the Minister of Railways submitted his statement he had not very much encouragement to'offer the House and the country, but he did promise that proper steps would be taken to apply business methods. Now, the Minister of Railways is a politician, and as such he stated that the only way to overcome deficits in connection with our railways was to increase the revenues, and the only way to increase the revenue is by increasing the rates. The deficit on the national railways does not fall on private shareholders but on the Canadian people, who have to meet it in taxation whether in the form of customs duties, income tax or taxes levied on the profits of business, and a deficit on the railways made up in this indirect way, which has to take the place of inadequate transportation rates, is unfair to the people.
The minister said last year that the management of the railways had urged the adoption of business methods and an advance in rates, but speaking for the Government, he got rid of this dilemma by

passing it on to Parliament and to the people. The rates were increased during the last year, however; but after all, notwithstanding these increased rates, the increased rates produced 19 per cent more revenue and advanced wages absorbed 16 per cent. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen opposite, when they talk about the railways, to say that we on this side are at fault because we have over-built; but I return the compliment and say that if we have over-built they have over-bought. Now, in view of the fact that the minister is not disposed to give us the information we want, we are obliged to take our own figures. I remember that in the Grand Trunk debate I submitted a detailed statement of operations and I challenged the Minister of Railways and the then Minister of the Interior, now Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) to refute them, but the right hon. gentleman declined to take the challenge up. I am sorry he is not in the House, but I shall have an opportunity at some time to repeat my challenge. Mr. Speaker, no one will buy these 11 p.m. railways, and the only thing we can do in the circumstances is to appoint a committee, secure all the information we can, and make the best of a bad job. I wrote a letter to Mr. Hanna asking that the Ocean Limited be allowed to make a regular stop, as it had always done in the past, at St. Charles de Belle-chasse. Any one who knows anything about the railways in the province of Quebec knows that this is an important station, also an initial station, but the Ocean Limited, instead of stopping at this station, simply slows down. I kept a record, covering a period of six months, of people who wanted to take the train to Montreal, but they had to take the Canadian Pacific railway from Quebec and then proceed; and although I did not give Mr. Hanna the figures, I may say that in six months the Canadian National Railways lost in this way the sum of $8,000. I told Mr. Hanna that I was prepared to do all I could to make the Canadian National Railways a success but he paid no heed to me. All these things could be inquired into if we had a proper committee.
It would be interesting to go into the question as to why the Canadian Northern people, when they handed their railway over to the Government, were allowed to keep strips of land along their line for which the Canadian National Railways today are held up; and it would also be interesting to know who disorganized the 114
Transcontinental. If the Transcontinental had been operated for the purpose for which it was built it would have been a great success. From the West to St. John it would have meant a shorter route by 440 miles. But instead seventy per cent of the production of western grain is taken to New York. I asked the Minister of Railways this afternoon who had lifted the rails of the Transcontinental and where they had gone to; and there are other things of great interest which would be brought out before a committee. I will not go further into these matters to-night. I shall have an opportunity to explain these and other things later on when the Estimates of the Minister of Railways are under consideration; but when I make this statement about the rails being lifted on the Transcontinental I make it on my own responsibility as a member of Parliament, and when the member for Bellechasse makes a statement he is prepared to substantiate it. The management of these railways has disorganized everything. This board disorganized the shops at Riviere du Loup by taking about 114 men from their homes there and planting them at the St. Malo shop, Quebec. Is that what my hon. friends opposite regard as a constructive measure? It is to inquire into matters of this kind that we want a committee. If the Government is not ashamed of the way in which these railways are being managed let us have a thorough investigation. Let us get at the facts and I am pre-' pared to do my share in futhering the necessary investigation.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I am extremely reluctant to keep the House, for even a minute or two, from a division so late upon a Friday night. I do not know that I should have intervened at all, because my position was stated perfectly from my point of view by my hon. friend from Marquette. If it had not been that my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) who represents the George Etienne Cartier division of Montreal made what I conceive to be a somewhat unjust attack upon my hon. friend near me. He charged him in so many words with having offered no constructive suggestions in regard to railroads in this country. Well I am not altogether sure that I agree with the constructive suggestions that my hon. friend from Marquette has made in their entirety as to their usefulness with regard to the railroad situation, but I had observed his doings carefully enough to notice that he



had at many joints in this country advocated a re-valuation of the railways for specific purposes. He did that in the city of my hon. friend from the division of George Etienne Cartier. In the same city he advocated a wise and well directed policy of immigration as a policy which might help the railroads of this country out of their difficulties. I mention these things to bring to my hon. friend's information up to date, and to repel his charge that my hon. friend from Marquette has not made constructive suggestions.
Sir, the course of the debates on railroad matters within the last two weeks ha3 been a little peculiar* and has debarred us from discussing the railroad question at large or I might have extended the constructive suggestions of my hon. friend considerably at the present moment. I will not do so however, because I have regard to the ruling which you, Sir, gave out at the beginning of this debate this afternoon, that the platform upon which we could speak to-day was a very narrow one. I am quite sure that with different occupants of the Chair this debate has gone far beyond the limits which you yourself, Sir, had in your mind at the moment, and I desire at this hour of the night to keep strictly to the question which is before the House. Now that question, like all new questions of this magnitude, presents a very great national difficulty, and I want to reiterate a statement which I have given expression to myself, and to emphasize it as it was expressed today by my hon. friend from Marquette-. a sentiment to the effect that our railroad difficulties are far too great for us to approach them except in the spirit of helpfulness and co-operation with a view to getting the nation through them.
The question before us to-day, in the form of the two motions upon which we shall presently decide by a vote, is a very difficult question. There are two considerations that are in the minds of all of us who are thinking earnestly upon the subject, and I think that is the case with every hon. gentleman in this House. We must have regard in the first place to the necessity of the management and directors of the National roads having that freedom and secrecy from day to day-and I emphasize the phrase "from day to day"- which are in the possession of the management and directors of all business corporations. Now, if the House was, as was proposed two weeks ago, to seek for itself, as a House of Commons, to exercise the power of so overlooking the management

and the directors of the National roads from day to day that they could pursue the ordinary course in regard to a Government department, then I am advised that the biggest railroad men on this continent would not take the job, because they would consider that they were foredoomed to failure owing to their operations being hampered and restricted in that way. For what would happen? I assume that even on occasion we should have some question directed to the Government on the Orders of the Day. They would either have to have that information, or they would immediately have to trouble the management about it when perhaps they were engaged in some other very important business. We should have questions put upon the Order Paper from day to day, we should have all the devices known to members of parliament, which would lead to the railroads being made a political football-all the devices usually used by members of parliament, I fear too often with a view to party or personal advantage rather than to the success of this great business enterprise which is being handled in a new way by this young country and is, I want to repeat, presenting us with problems of the very greatest difficulty.
On the other hand, there must be present to the minds of all of us another necessity which, to my mind, is equally urgent, and that is the necessity of Parliament and the people-who are the shareholders of these roads-being possessed of the means of exercising a vigilant oversight over the handling of their property. If they have not the means of that oversight, Mr. Speaker, it is clear even to a tyro in matters of business, that slackness in the management will inevitably creep in, that business evils will creep in, and-as some have anticipated-our deficiencies, our deficits, will rise instead of falling as the days go by. Well now, the Government have thought it wise to make an attempt along that line by proposing in the first place, that we should relieve ourselves of the difficulties to which I first alluded by appointing a committee of this House to make inquiries under certain very definite restrictions.
May I say at once, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot see what would be the use of that committee at all operating under those restrictions. It is proposed to confine the work of this committee to making up their minds what information, if any, should be given to the House of Commons, and the methods by which that information should be com-

municated. Well, I am bound to say that if that be all the committee is to do, that is something which the House of Commons surely has the power to decide for itself here and now. And, holding that view, I shall vote for the amendment.
I asked my right hon. friend, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), when he was speaking, how a committee could possibly decide on what information ought to be communicated to the House if the committee itself knew nothing about the information at all or was to be restricted in the information which it did have. If the committee is to be restricted in respect to the information which it possesses, it would baffle the human intelligence of this committee to form a sensible opinion on what information should be given to this House. The committee would meet in ignorance, it would deliberate in ignorance, and it would decide in ignorance if it were restricted in the way in which this motion proposes. So that I repeat I cannot see what the use of a committee working under these restrictions would be at all. On the other hand, if they choose, as doubtless; the Government will, a committee of men of parliamentary experience-most of our committees do have hon. gentlemen of considerable parliamentary experience chosen by preference-and, in addition hon. members who have devoted their attention largely to railroad matters, then I am with the demand that they should have the power to get what information seems to them wise as a parliamentary committee.
I would only add, in conclusion, that I should think they would exercise those powers with discretion. I understood my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) to say in his remarks to the House to-day that we should rely on the discretion of such a parliamentary committee conducting its inquiries with a view to the two necessities which they would have peculiarly placed upon them-the necessity, on the one hand, of not unduly hampering the management and directors of the road; and, on the other hand, the necessity of bringing to Parliament at least sufficient information to enable it to exercise a vigilant oversight of those who are managing this great national property.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Clark), it is my purpose to be very brief at this stage of the debate. I find myself in sympathy with the resolution before the House, but before recording my vote I should like to
114|
ask my right hon friend, the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), two questions, which he will have an opportunity to answer when closing the debate. In the first place, I would call to his attention the fact that when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) was presenting his report to this House he referred specifically to the high wages paid the railway employees as being one cause of the large deficits. I should like to ask my right hon. friend if I am right in assuming that the wage earners of the railroad will be given an opportunity to present their side of that question before this proposed committee? The second question I would ask my right hon. friend is this: Will the gentlemen who recently came from Winnipeg to present their case before the Board of Railway Commissioners relative to railway rates be given an opportunity to re-state their case before this committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answering the hon. member I would like also to make a few remarks anent the amendment itself. The fixing of wages or of rates could not, no matter whether the amendment or the motion passed, come within the jurisdiction of the committee. The first matter is necessarily in charge of the Canadian National Railway Company on the one side and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the other; and the control of rates is delegated by statute specifically to the Railway Commission. But the men employed on the road could personally or through their organizations give evidence before the committee as to anything that the committee is deputed to ascertain, and among the things deputed to it the question of the form of the annual report and what it should disclose would be something upon which they could be called and could give evidence, as well as on any other subject within the purview of the committee. I do want to say a word too, as to the peculiar position this House would be in if it accepted this amendment. I do not know that I can make it any clearer than it was, to me at least, stated in the speech of the right hon. gentleman the member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden). It will be recalled that in previous debates-and I do not wish to refer to them again in extenso-it was very generally conceded, and particularly by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), in language that to my judgment was precisely right, that unquestionably there is information as to operation in respect to which the management must

have the same secrecy and control as the management of any other system, and which information, as expressed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), will not be subject to disclosure in Parliament while the operation is going on. For example, supposing we should have to disclose in Parliament the shipments made by a certain firm of their particular line of goods, manufactured perhaps in Chicago or at some other point served by our roads, will any hon. member for a moment suggest that this House would be justified in publishing that information? But it is a matter of operation and is within the meaning of this amendment. And so with other matters. I am told that if the management were to make known the differentials as to the rates given, it would make operation impossible, that is, they would not get the business and the loss would be disastrous to the system. I can pass from one thing to another, and in each instance 1 can assure the House that if the information is disclosed it will add millions of dollars to the deficit. There is no question ' in the world about it. I do not need to argue it with the hon. member for Marquette, who has himself stated in language that he would be expected to use as the manager himself of a large business concern. Now, we will suppose this amendment passes. Then where are we landed as respects this very information that the hon. member says cannot be disclosed without disaster? What is the duty of this committee, if it is appointed, what is it entrusted to do, yea, deputed to do by this Parliament? Is it deputed to bring in a recommendation as to anything? Has it any definite purpose? None whatever; it is not asked to do anything; it is not asked to help us in any respect whatever. It is simply asked to inquire into-what? Info all matters that in any way relate to the railways owned and controlled by the Government. It was suggested by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that the committee would not take the position of permitting anything and everything to be inquired into. But suppose some member got up in that committee and said: I want to know these things that the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) says should not be known; that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's says it could not be conceived that any committee would disclose. Suppose that member of the committee said: I want to call a witness to find that out-who could rise in 
the committee and say, "no"? This House told the committee to get the information.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend a question to elucidate the matter? Would it not be entirely proper for the committee to exercise its discretion in the matter?

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
No, decidedly it would not. Hon. members say "hear, hear," but they know it would not. It is in the motion; that is why the motion is worded as it is-worded to say that the committee may ascertain anything that the committee deems it necessary to inquire into. If this amendment passes the committee is deputed to inquire into everything connected with the road, and no chairman of that committee and no member of it would be doing his duty who would get up and say that the committee had any right to prevent the disclosure of anything whatever relating to that railway. How would he have the right? Upon what would he base his right? Would he say: I know better; I know that will do harm? Oh, the reply would be, Parliament has told us to inquire into everything; that is what we are here for. Parliament has not given us any discretion; it has told us to go so far as we deem necessary. Parliament does not tell the committee to go as far as it may deem necessary for certain purposes. No purpose is set out in this amendment. The committee are to be sent out into the wilderness and told that they have power-indeed it is their duty to go into anything that anybody wants to go into-and hon. members boast that that is the power which is given to the committee. And once any information under such a reference gets before that committee it is before this House; it is in the press the same day. Everything may be done that hon. members have said must not be done if we are to have any regard at all for efficient management and for the success of the system.
Now, I do not think the hon. member for Marquette understood-there is a habit in this House of sprniging these things suddenly-he did not understand that that was the effect of the amendment. But that is the effect, and that is precisely why the amendment was worded as it is. The only thing that approached an argument in this matter-I do not want to use the language discourteously-or that appealed to me as being most within the region of relevancy was something urged by the member for Sunbury and Queen's.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman try to- get that right, now? It is Shelburne and Queen's.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; I shall be glad to give it the right designation. There will be a member for Sunbury very soon, but he will be on this side of the House.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The hon. member is
not going to give him a chance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: There will be no mistaking him.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: When he comes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
And he will come. My hon. friend's contention was with regard to pensions. The committee, he said, was given carte blanche to make any recommendations to the House that it thought best with regard to pensions and civil reestablishment. That is true, and if the same course could safely have been pursued here it would have been done. But the reason why it could not safely have been pursued here is just the reason which was urged in such strong terms by the hon. member for Marquette; as regards pensions, those reasons would not apply at all. It is because there was the necessity for protecting the management in the running of their concern that restraint was necessary here where no restraint was necessary in respect to pensions. There was nothing that could not be disclosed with respect to pensions at any time without hurting anybody, and that is just the difference.
Now, let me repeat: if we adopt a resolution establishing a committee which shall have power to inquire into all matters relating to the railways owned and controlled by the Government, that makes it a committee so to do, and in order to get information on any subject all a member of the committee has to do is assert in the committee that the subject into which he wishes to inquire relates to the railways owned and controlled by the Government, and he has no right to be stopped. Does the hon. member say that in the Pensions committee, which had a similar deputed power, any one could have prevented an inquiry into any matter relating to pensions? Certainly no one had the power to do so, and the chairman of the committee would have been derelict in his duty if he had prevented any such inquiry. It is the same here.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Will the right hon.
gentleman permit me a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Does he think that when a committee has the right to exercise a certain power, it is obliged to exercise it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Why, no, it is not
obliged to do it; for that matter, the committee does not need to meet. No one is going to exercise physical force to make them do it. But what I say is that if any member of the committee wished to go into any matter, the chairman of the committee, under the authority given in the amendment, has no right whatever to resist it.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman permit me a question before he leaves that point? A few moments ago an hon. member brought to the attention of the House a question regarding the closing of a small station in the province of Quebec, a question which he wanted to argue before the committee. Could that be done under the terms of the amendment? He declared that that was exactly what they wanted to do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: There would be nothing in the world to prevent its being discussed and information brought out concerning it, so long as it related to the road.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: If the committee gave its consent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Under the amendment the committee has no discretion.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me a question? If the Committee on Public Accounts should endeavour to get information respecting the private and confidential business transactions which a merchant carries on with a customer, what would happen? The committee have the power to go into that, but they will not do it; neither would the committee in this case be unreasonable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: It does not matter how private and confidential it is; if it affects the public business and a member of the committee takes an aff davit that it does, the Committee on Public Accounts does not prevent him from going into it.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: They have the right to refuse, and would always do it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Not at all, if the public interest was affected. I never knew it to be refused, and I sat on the Public Accounts Committee for many years. It

is for Parliament to say what shall be within the discretion of the committee. If there is no need for restraint, there will be none; if there is need for restraint, it is for Parliament to say so when it constitutes the committee.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend if the committee under the Government's resolution would have the right to seek any information at all about the management of the road?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: Yes. I am glad the hon. member rose, because I know that he too is under a misconception. The hon. member at the close of his speech indicated that there was some restraint put on the committee in the reaching for evidence to enable it to come to the conclusions that are therein set out. Under the main motion the committee is under no restraint at all; it can inquire into anything it thinks necessary to inquire into that will assist it in arriving at conclusions on the subjects that are set before it.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: If the committee is to have the power to seek information, why restrict it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: The committee has definite objects; it has the discretion to say whether any inquiry is necessary to enable it to reach the objects set out. That discretion is given it by resolution. But in this amendment no objects whatever are set out; the committee is simply given the duty of inquiring into anything at all that relates to the railways.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: If the committee sees fit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The amendment does not say that; it provides that anything relating to the railways may be gone into. If there were any object set out and it was provided that the committee could decide whether or not it was necessary to go into anything in order to reach that object, that would be all right. But no purposes are set out here; it is merely a blind resolution. It turns the committee out in the dark, and all the committee has to do is to hunt around and see if it cannot find something for no purpose which the committee knows anything about. That is put forward in order to get in this House some votes that will, if possible, vote down the Government's motion.
My contention is that the Government has submitted this motion in good faith

for definite, concrete purposes and has made it as wide as there was any possibility of making it, if any regard is to be had for the wisdom of leaving the management some opportunity to make the road a success. If no regard is to be had for that, as hon. gentlemen immediately opposite argue, then certainly there would be no need for any restraint; but if regard is to be had for that, then we have made the very least possible restraint that you can make. I have submitted this, I know, not with any hope that I will change the vote of any hon. member who has declared himself; I could not expect that; but I lay it before the House in the hope that I will change their minds or, at least, give them some grounds for reflection whether they are on solid ground or not, and certainly with the hope that I will convince them that the Government has nothing in the world to conceal for its own purposes; that it has submitted this in the utmost good faith as the furthest step that can be taken, and the best designed to get real-and useful results for the country.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to this debate will be a brief one, and I will endeavour to confine myself strictly to the point at issue. In the latter regard I know that I will have your cordial good wishes.
Adverting to what was said by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in the last of his many admirable speeches, may 1 point out to him, with all respect, that as regards the fears Which he has expressed of what would happen if we had what is called parliamentary control, or House of Commons control, of the railway systems of this country, his argument proceeded upon the basis that such a thing apparently had never existed. The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) enlarged upon that and pictured, for the purpose of creating bogeys to frighten his friends angularly opposite, some terrible things that might ensue. For over fifty years we had parliamentary and House of Commons management of the Intercolonial, and none of the things which were pictured here this evening and this afternoon has ever happened.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext: All of them happened.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE
speechtext:
There was no interference with people; there was no disclosure of information that militated against the Intercolonial. Matters were carried out in a regular and businesslike way through the responsible department. The head of that department made his statement to l'arlia-

ment, came before Parliament and was interrogated in the usual way regarding the details of his administration of the department and of the railroad committed to his care, so that we are not at all without precedent in connection with that phase of the matter.

subtopic: REPERENCE TO SPECIAL, COMMITTEE OP THE HOUSE

speechtext:
If the Government
really desired, through a series of questions to be submitted to a committee to give effect to what is in the mind of the Canadian people at the present time in regard to the railway situation, these are the questions that ought to be submitted to their proposed committee:
(1)	What is the total amount of the present railway deficit?
(2)	What are the causes that produced that deficit?
(3)	What remedy should be applied to prevent a recurrence of railway deficits?
Then, if the Government further desired to go about the matter in a thorougly practical way, they would invest the committee with the powers prescribed in the
amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition. But the Government has done nothing of the kind. Instead of submitting practical questions of that kind to be determined by this committee, the Government proposes to submit a set of questions that will entail prolonged discusssion, endless hair-splitting, and, in the end, no practical results. One has only to read the questions to see that standing out in all its nakedness before him. Let me read them:
(1)	What information as to operation of Canadian National Railways and Shipping as conducted by the Board of Directors and Management should, in the public interest, be brought down in Parliament on Question, Motion for Production of Papers, or otherwise.
(2)	When, by that method, and under what conditions, if any, should such information be given, regard being had for the necessity of securing to Parliament and the public all facts requisite for the determination of policy (including finance), and to the Board of Directors the best possible conditions for efficiency of management.
(3)	What system of auditing should be adopted, and what extent of detail should be given in the Annual Report.
(4)	Whether and for what purposes the said committee should be continued, and that for the above purposes and for such other purposes as the committee deem in the public interest there be referred to said committee the Annual Report of the Board of Directors and that the said committee have power to examine witnesses under oath, to send for papers, persons, and records, and to report from time to time.
That is not the kind of information that the Canadian people are looking for at the present time and expect this Parliament to obtain. The people expect, yea, the people demand the fullest possible information on the railway situation. On that score, there is complete agreement between those who advocate public ownership and those who advocate private ownership and operation of railways. In support of that, let me read a few extracts from a couple of editorials published immediately after the preceding debate in this House upon this subject. On March 24, last, the Toronto Globe said:
In his speech on the condition of the Government railways Dr. Reid made an appeal for advice as to how the situation could be improved. Obviously the House could not respond to the appeal unless it were put in possession of the facts, and from this point of view there was force in Mr. King's amendment asserting the right of Parliament to full information as to the working of the railways. The taxpayers, who will have to make good a deficit of nearly $70,000,000 this year, have also a right to be informed. The objection that information of this kind might give an unfair advantage to the Canadian Pacific railway, a formidable rival of the Government railways, has not a great

deal of weight. The success of the C.P.K. has much more solid foundation than the obtaining of an occasional glimpse into the business of its rivals. Nor is it fair to assume tha/t the amendment moved by the Opposition was actuated by hostility to Government ownership. Public ownership must be accompanied by publicity and responsibility.
i
Further in the same article the Globe says:
What the House and the country require is not fragmentary information as to details, hut a clear understanding of the working of the system, its weaknesses and their causes, with a view to finding a remedy i-f possible. This is not to be found either in the annual statements of the Minister of Railways or in any accounts or other information submitted to Parliament. Government ownership on so vast a scale is a new departure, and new means of communicating information must be devised.
Still later the same editorial goes on:
The general principle that the House should control the expenditure of public money applies as much to railways as to any other branch of the public business. Public ownership does not mean, or should not mean, the denial of one of the first principles of responsible government.
And again:
The vastness of the system and the huge expenditures it involves are reasons, not for less, but for more information.
Then on the same date the Montreal Gazette, an exponent of the principle of private ownership and operation of railways had this to say in an editorial:
Perhaps as good an illustration as can be found to prove that the National railway has been taken out of politics is the proposed appointment of a Parliamentary Committee to bring it into, politics. The absurd pretence that the property of the people can be turned over to an irresponsible Board of Directors compelled the Prime Minister to take up a wrong attitude towards the amendment of Hon. Mr.' King on Tuesday evening. The constitutional principle which the leader of the Oppositon invited the House to approve is absolutely unassailable, that principle being "that it is the undoubted right of Parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, accounts, correspondence and papers in relation to the management of every department of the public service, including the affairs of the Canadian National railways, whether operating directly under the control of a department or under corporate form."
The Government treated Hon. Mr. King's amendment as tantamount to a vote of want of confidence, and as a consequence it was rejected; yet the principle that the people who pay the taxes have a right to know how the proceeds of the taxes are applied survives.
The pretension that to submit the National railway management to the Inquisition of Parliament might lead to divulging of important business secrets to the Canadian Pacific Company is not to be taken seriously. We imagine the executive officers of the Canadian Pacific will not sit at the feet of the National Railway Board to learn wisdom. The point, however, is

this: who owns the National railways; out of whose pockets come the money to make up the operating and interest charges of that system? The people of Canada own the roads; they and they alone are the proprietors and if the management has been entrusted to half a dozen or more reputable gentlemen, does that deprive the owners of the right to demand an accounting? The truth is that the Government made a false step when it set up the pretence that the National railway was taken out of politics by intrusting its affairs to a government-appointed Board. The National railway has not been taken out of politics; it cannot be taken out of politics; and it should not be taken out of politics. As well contend that the Canadian Pacific Directorate, or that any other corporate institution should not be amenable to its shareholders. It is the last thing to be tolerated that a dozen gentlemen, however estimable, should be given a free hand to do as they will with the property of the people. The Government is accountable to Parliament for its administration of public affairs; why should that accountibility be removed from the men who manage' the largest and most important branch of the public service?
The editorial concludes with this statement:
The question is of supreme importance, and the sooner the Government drops the flimsy pretence that the responsibility for the management of the people's railways has been committed to an irresponsible directorate, and is therefore immune from criticism, the sooner will the country arrive at a solution of its most difficult and disturbing problem.
So that the position taken by the hon. leader of the Opposition, as expressed in the amendment that is now before the House, is endbrsed as I have said by those who advocate public ownership, as well as by those who advocate private ownership of these great public utilities.
Now, Sir, up to the time the right hon. gentleman the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) spoke this afternoon, the discussion had proceeded on the assumption that this Government committee which the Government proposes would investigate something, but the right hon. the member for King's made it quite plain that this committee would not investigate anything. In so doing he destroyed practically all the arguments that had been advanced in support of the Government's position up to that time, and he also took the force out of the argument which the leader of the Government addressed to the House just a few moments ago. What did the hon. member for King's say? In rather vigorous language he criticized the position taken by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in supporting the amendment, and in doing that he made the definite statement, a very proper statement, I submit, that the purpose of this proposed committee is not to conduct an investigation, but to

define a principle. That, Sir, I submit, is precisely the fact, but that, Sir, I again submit, is not what the people of this country expect of any such committee at this present time, and, Sir, in view of that fact, I commend not only the wisdom of my hon. friend from Marquette, and his friends who sit about him, in supporting this amendment, but the greater wisdom of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in embodying these sound principles in the resolution which he has placed in your hands.
Then the right hon. gentleman from King's said that after defining a principle, and he took good care not to say how many weeks or how many months it would take the committee to define this principle, the committee could come to this House and ask for powers to carry out this principle. Now may I inquire how long the Government intends that this farce should go on? How long is this performance to be kept up about defining a principle and then coming back to this House to find out how you are going to apply that principle, when, and to whom? If the Government are allowed a free hand in the matter, I venture the prophesy, that the leader of the Government will not be able to get away to the Imperial Conference in June next, because long after that time this House will be deliberating some feature of this principle which is to be defined by this committee. Now is it not apparent to everybody who has given a moment's thought to the subject that while the Canadian people are hungering for the facts about the railways, this proposed committee, limited to these four questions, will spend its time debating theories and in discussing academic issues? This committee will not only spend its time in doing that, but in bringing in interim reports to this House, and further time will be taken up in discussing these reports here and in issuing further instructions to this committee. Then in the end what will happen? My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) expressed grave regret this afternoon that somebody on this side of the House should have even mentioned the prospect of a majority and a minority report. Well, it is not so many years ago that my hon. friend and I served on the Soldiers Boots Committee of this House, and I recall with a good deal of pleasure that he was then very glad to join in a minority report when the majority in the committee undertook to stifle the facts and prevent them from
being known to the House. So majority and minority reports are not as strange to my hon. friend from North Oxford as he would lead the House to believe.
There will be time spent in doing all these things. Then a debate will take place in this House, after the majority and minority reports are brought in here, and finally the majority report will be endorsed by the majority supporting the Government in this House. Well, Mr. Speaker, what period of the year do you think we shall have reached then? We will have gone long past the time when the right hon. gentleman should have sailed for the Imperial Conference, and the country which at this moment expects us to be busy eliciting the facts as to the total amount of the railway deficit and the causes contributing to that deficit, and studying means for providing a remedy to prevent a recurrence of that deficit-the country that expects us to do that will by that time have become so disgusted with this Parliament that the force of public opinion will, I believe, drive these gentlemen to the polls no matter how disinclined they may be to face the electorate.
The situation has been referred to as a serious one. Of course it is. Nothing could be more serious than the railway situation that confronts us to-day. But how is it possible that there should fall from the lips of hon. gentlemen who pictured the gravity of the situation, the proposition that the time of this House and of a committee embodying a large number of members from every section of the House should be occupied in debating theories, in defining a principle, instead of going into matters in a businesslike way and ascertaining the facts. I am glad to see my hon.' friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) coming to his seat; he also expressed the hope that this committee would be composed of business men. In that remark I find an echo of some observations heard in this House a few days ago regarding the desirability of having business men and not lawyers on this committee or similar committees. Well, I may point out to my hon. friend from Oxford that a lawyer is the head of the most successful transportation system in this country, if not in the world. The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway is a lawyer; and I might also point out to my hon. friend and those who entertain this idea, that a business man has been the head of the institution that has made the mess we are called upon to deal with at the present time in connection with the Canadian National

Railway system. A lawyer is also the head of the great United States Steel Corporation, one of the best managed and most successful institutions in the world; while a business man made the terrible mess of the railway situation in the United States. I could go further in this connection, but it is unnecessary to extend the argument.

speechtext:
Before the main motion is put I should like to suggest to my right hon. friend the leader of the Government that the motion might well be enlarged in one particular, and I propose to offer an amendment to that effect. I will take only a minute or two in suggesting one or two reasons for it. One of the essential needs to final success in the operation of our national railways and merchant marine, is the complete establishment of confidence on the part of the public in the management and control of the enterprise, and I am bound to say that that confidence will, in large measure, depend upon the freedom from political influence of any kind with the proper administration of the system. Only in such a way also can complete efficiency in management be secured. Now under the present method of handling this matter, the appointment of the Board of Directors, and consequently the control of the management, lies in the hands of the Government. I am not here offering any criticism of the Government for the manner in which that responsibility has been discharged by them in the past, but nevertheless I wish to point out the fact that so long as that condition obtains, whether it is under the present Government or any Government that succeeds it, the possibility of that power being used by the Government of the day for political ends will be present in the minds of a great many people in this country, and it is very desirable, Sir, that it be removed if possible from them.
Now, I quite recognize the difficulty that confronts one in the consideration of this question. It has been said to-night that the people of Canada are the shareholders in this railway system, and that is absolutely and entirely true. At the same time they cannot discharge the functions that are ordinarily discharged by shareholders in a private corporation. On the other hand if the matter is left entirely in the control of the Government, the abuses that I have already referred to will arise as far as the election of directors are concerned and the appointment of the management. It seems to me therefore, Sir, that it would

be well if my right hon. friend who leads the Government would consent to an enlargement of the powers of this committee in one particular, and to that end-without any desire to keep the House sitting any longer because I trust I have made my position clear in the short statement I have made-I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) :
That the motion he amended by adding thereto as clause 5, the following words:
What aproximation, if any, consistent with the responsibility of Parliament in the matter, can be found to the appointment and the control of directors and management ordinarily exercised by shareholders in a private corporation.
I think this is a matter that might well engage the attention of the committee. If we are to reach any sound settlement of this very important question it must, I think, be found, if possible, along the lines I have indicated. I could extend my remarks and amplify the argument in favour of this amendment; but I do not wish to do so at this late hour; it would be a hardship on the House after we have spent so many hours to-day in debate. Therefore, I submit this amendment to my right hon. friend in the best of faith and with an honest desire to help, and I trust he may see his way clear to accept it.

Will you accept the
amendment?
Mr. MEIGHEN; I find myself in general agreement with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), Mr. Speaker, as regards the object that he has in view, and I am glad to say that I am able to give him another evidence that my argument was correct on the motion in chief, by assuring him that I am prepared to accept the amendment in wider terms than he puts it. Among the subjects to be deputed to the committee for inquiry he suggests:
What approximation, if any, consistent with the responsibility of Parliament in the matter can be found to the appointment and to the control of directors and management ordinarily exercised by shareholders in a private corporation.
What the hon. member has in mind, if I read his amendment correctly, is as to whether or not there might not be appointed in some way some body which would take the place usually occupied by shareholders in relation to a private concern. That is the suggestion the hon. member makes as to a possible improvement in the plan that Parliament has adopted for

*
the management of the system. I would suggest to him that it would be better to make it wider, so as to include not only any recommendation the committee might see fit to make along the line of his amendment, but along any line at all that the committee might feel would be a suggestion looking to the improvement of the general scheme of management. I intimated when the matter was first before the House, that that might be well submitted as a suitable subject for inquiry by the committee, and1 I know the hon. member will admit in a moment that if it is to be a subject for inquiry, while it should of course be definite, still keeping it definite it should be as wide as it can be made. If, for example, the committee should feel that the Board of Directors might be differently appointed, without establishing any body to take the place of shareholders, or if they might have any other recommendation that they saw fit after inquiry to make, that would enable Parliament to improve the general scheme of management of the system, it should be recommended. The plan now is to appoint, by the Government, a Board of Directors of business men, a president and general manager. If there is any better plan, whether it is along the line the hon. member suggests by his amendment or not, then if this committee can recommend it, it will be of advantage to this House.
I have re-drafted the amendment myself in these words, which I think cover the ground:
What, if any, improvement could he made in the general scheme of management.
That undoubtedly would enable the com-mitte, if they saw fit, to report in favour of just such a plan as the hon. member intimates is in his mind by the amendment that he moves, and it would enable the committee, if they thought there was anything better or anything additional to that, to recommend that as well. I am prepared to accept the amendment in that form. I do not think it would be put in the best shape just in the way it is submitted by the hon. member, first, because it is too confined, and, second because I do not know that the expression means in the ultimate just exactly what the hon member intended it to mean.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution of my right hon. friend related primarily to discovering the methods whereby information could be given to Parliament in respect to the management, control and operation of these National railways. The amendment which is now proposed has to do not so much with the question of information, which is the one that we have been discussing throughout the day, as it has with considering a different method of control and management. As such, it seems to me that it introduces an entirely new subject for the consideration of the committee.
I have already pointed out that I thought the object of the Government in instituting the committee was to get away entirely from the question of disclosing information as fully as this House wishes to have it, and to substitute a series of other questions for the committee to consider. This
amendment adds just one more to the list. Much more time of the committee will now be taken up in considering questions of management and control, and we shall probably be put off further than ever from getting the information which we wish to receive. On the other hand, if there is going to be a committee I suppose there is no harm in referring to it any number of questions. The subject dealt with in the amendment now proposed is an important one, which might well be debated in Parliament at any time. But if the reference of one additional question to the committee will have the effect of assisting the Government to discover a policy for itself, I for one have no objection to its addition. At the same time, I should say that the committee as a whole is not acceptable to us on this side of the House, because it is not a committee with power to get full information and to get it at once, but is rather, as I have already stated, a committee for the purpose of engaging in studies of an academic character. While I do not think the, proposed committee will meet the purposes which we have in view, there is not enough objection to the reference to it of the additional question to warrant our asking the House to divide on the amendment.

is adopted I should like to say a word. It would seem from the discussion to-night that this resolution as drafted is not sufficient to meet the requirements of the situation. We are all looking for a solution of this question. Hon. members opposite accuse the Opposition of playing politics, but certainly hon. gentlemen on this side have had no hand in the playing of politics in regard to these railways. It is the earnest desire of every member of the Opposition, I am sure, to find a solution. I think the Prime Minister should consider some method of arriving at a com-

mittee that would have complete power to handle this whole question.

Toronto, April 7, 1921.
Dear Dr. Reid :-Referring to my letter of yesterday's date, enclosing answers to questions asked in the House by Hon. Mr. Murphy, relative to wages paid on the Canadian Rational railways.
You will note answer to Question No. 4, showing the monthly earnings paid to certain classes of employees, is based on the regular working hours, but in order to show the effect of the overtime conditions, I am enclosing herewith a memorandum, in duplicate, giving total earnings of twelve agent-operators at different points on the eastern lines of Canadian Northern railway for the years 1916-20, which you may wish to add to our answer to Question No. 4.
Yours very truly,

Question 4 of the series asked by Hon. Charles Murphy (Russell) on 7th instant, is as follows:
4.	"What are the monthly earnings as compared with 1916 for the following classes of employees working full regular working hours:-Shop Mechanics, Carmen, Agents and Operators, Freight Shed Men, Trackmen, Bridge and Building Men?
The statements given in answer to the series of questions, including the No. 4 above, will be found appended to the Debates of 7th instant. The supplementary statement ordered to be published in the present issue follows:	.
Question 4-
Memorandum
The earnings per month shown for the various classes of employees are exclusive of overtime for emergency service. We are, however, showing below a state-inent prepared for the years 1916 and 1920 showing the total earnings of 12 agents, which will show that the total earnings are greatly affected by overtime conditions. We would, however, point out the stations referred to were some of the stations where the highest amount of overtime had been paid, and does not mean that every station would be affected the same way, as far as the individual earnings are concerned, as at points where it is found more economical to add an extra operator it is done, rather than pay overtime. However, the expense to the Railway is practically the same whether it is paid in overtime or for additional staff, due to the eighthourday.
